stories.title: Delhi court sentences former AAP councillor Tahir Hussain to life imprisonment for murdering an IB officer in the 2020 riots
stories.what_happened: On **Friday, July 31**, the Karkardooma Court convicted **Tahir Hussain and four others** under India's murder law along with rioting and kidnapping charges, and sentenced all five to **life imprisonment** for Sharma's killing. The court held that Hussain was part of a mob that assembled with clear intent to riot and attack, and imposed a **₹5 lakh fine** on him. Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, but the court ruled the crime — while heinous — did not cross the legal threshold requiring it. The verdict caps a trial that ran for more than **five years** since the 2020 riots. Sharma's brother has publicly said the family will appeal for the death penalty.
key_points: Delhi's **Karkardooma Court** sentenced **Tahir Hussain** and four co-accused to **life imprisonment** for the 2020 murder of Intelligence Bureau officer **Ankit Sharma**.
The court rejected the prosecution's demand for the **death penalty**, ruling the case didn't meet the 'rarest of rare' threshold.
Hussain, a former **AAP councillor** who later joined AIMIM, was convicted of murder, rioting and kidnapping, and fined **₹5 lakh**.
Sharma's body was found in a **drain** near Hussain's house during the riots; Sharma's brother is now demanding the **death penalty** on appeal.

depth.background: The **2020 Delhi riots** were the capital's worst communal violence in decades, triggered by clashes over the Citizenship Amendment Act; they killed over **50 people** across northeast Delhi in late February 2020. Ankit Sharma, an Intelligence Bureau officer, went missing during the riots and was later found dead in a drain, allegedly killed by a mob. Tahir Hussain, then a sitting AAP councillor from the area, was accused of being part of that mob and was arrested soon after; he denied wrongdoing throughout the more than five-year trial and later left AAP to contest elections for AIMIM.

stories.title: Cabinet approves India's biggest-ever sports push: ₹36,441 crore to revamp Khelo India and fund national federations
stories.what_happened: The Union Cabinet approved a **revamped Khelo India Scheme** alongside enhanced **Assistance to National Sports Federations (ANSFs)**, with a combined financial outlay of **₹36,441 crore** running from **2026-27 through 2030-31**. Of that, **₹29,054 crore** is allocated to Khelo India to build a talent pipeline from the grassroots up, while **₹7,387 crore** goes to federation support — funding coaching, sports science, modern equipment, engagement of foreign experts, training camps, and participation in major international competitions. The government describes the combined package as roughly **eight times** the scale of the previous Khelo India investment, and as the country's **most ambitious sports development programme since Independence**. Officials framed the investment explicitly around India's bid to host the **2036 Olympics** and its role as host of the **2030 Commonwealth Games** in Ahmedabad, aiming to build a continuous pipeline from grassroots talent to Olympic medals.
key_points: The Union Cabinet approved a combined **₹36,441 crore** outlay for a revamped **Khelo India Scheme** and enhanced support to **National Sports Federations (NSFs)**, running through 2030-31.
**₹29,054 crore** goes to Khelo India itself — building a pipeline of talented athletes starting at the **grassroots level**.
**₹7,387 crore** is earmarked for federation support: coaching, sports science, modern equipment, foreign experts, and international competition exposure.
The government calls it roughly **8 times the previous Khelo India investment**, and its most ambitious sports program **since Independence**.
It's explicitly timed to India's push to host the **2036 Olympics** and build on momentum from the **2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad**.

depth.background: **Khelo India** is the federal government's flagship program for building sporting talent from school level upward, launched in 2018 to address India's historically thin medal hauls relative to its population. India has been on an upward athletic trajectory — a record medal count at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, including breakthrough performances in boxing and judo — and has separately been formally pursuing a bid to host the **2036 Olympics**. Sports federations (NSFs) are the bodies that govern individual sports (athletics, boxing, wrestling, etc.) and have long complained of being underfunded relative to what international competitiveness requires.

stories.title: India's Cabinet approves a ₹5,070 crore scheme to build floating solar power plants on lakes, dams and reservoirs
stories.what_happened: The **Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi**, approved the **Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY)** — a new scheme to build **floating solar photovoltaic projects with co-located energy storage systems** — with a total financial outlay of **₹5,070 crore**. The scheme targets **5,000 MW of floating solar capacity** paired with a minimum of **two hours of battery storage (10,000 MWh)**, to be built on **reservoirs, dams, lakes, industrial ponds and other inland water bodies** across the country. Projects will be sanctioned from **FY2026-27 through FY2030-31**, with financial support disbursed up to **FY2032-33**. Developers will receive **Central Financial Assistance of ₹1 crore per commissioned megawatt**, and can separately claim up to **₹50 lakh per project** to cover feasibility studies like bathymetry and hydrography surveys. The government projects the scheme will cut roughly **10 million tonnes of CO2 emissions annually** and create **16,000–17,000 jobs**.
key_points: The **Pradhan Mantri Surya Sarovar Yojana (PM-SSY)** targets **5,000 MW of floating solar capacity** paired with battery storage, backed by a **₹5,070 crore** outlay.
Storage requirement: every project must include at least **2 hours (10,000 MWh total) of co-located battery storage**, so power keeps flowing after sunset.
Developers get **₹1 crore per MW** in central funding once a project is commissioned, plus up to **₹50 lakh per project** for feasibility studies.
Panels will float on **reservoirs, dams, lakes and industrial ponds** instead of using farmland — sparing land that's often scarce or contested.
The scheme is projected to cut **10 million tonnes of CO2 emissions a year** and create **16,000–17,000 jobs**, running from FY2026-27 through FY2032-33.

depth.background: India has been racing to expand **renewable energy capacity** to meet ambitious 2030 climate targets, but conventional ground-mounted solar farms compete with agricultural and residential land — a genuine friction point in a densely populated country. **Floating solar** sidesteps that by putting panels on water bodies instead, with the added bonus that water cooling makes the panels run more efficiently than on land, and evaporation from reservoirs is reduced by the shade. India already has some floating solar pilots, but nothing at this scale or with mandatory battery storage attached, which addresses solar's biggest limitation: it doesn't generate power at night.

stories.title: India's Cabinet approves a ₹36,441 crore overhaul of the Khelo India sports scheme, betting big after its best-ever Commonwealth Games showing
stories.what_happened: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved an expanded Khelo India Scheme along with enhanced Assistance to National Sports Federations (ANSFs), with a combined outlay of **₹36,441 crore** running from **2026-27 through 2030-31** — up from an earlier five-year allocation of roughly ₹29,000 crore. Information and Broadcasting Minister **Ashwini Vaishnaw** announced the decision, which introduces new programs including **Khelo India Feeder Schools** and **Utkrishta Vidyalayas** (excellence-focused schools) meant to identify talented young athletes earlier and track them through a structured development pipeline. The scheme also creates an **'Emerging Khelo India Athletes'** category that expands the pool of athletes eligible for state support by roughly **ten times** its previous size. The decision comes as India's contingent has its best-ever Commonwealth Games campaign in Glasgow, with a record number of boxing finalists and medals across multiple sports.
key_points: The Union Cabinet approved a revamped **Khelo India Scheme** with a combined outlay of **₹36,441 crore** for **2026-27 to 2030-31**.
It replaces an earlier five-year plan that had a smaller **₹29,000 crore** outlay.
New initiatives include **Khelo India Feeder Schools** and **Utkrishta Vidyalayas**, building a pipeline from school sport to the Olympic podium.
The eligible athlete pool expands **nearly ten-fold** through a new 'Emerging Khelo India Athletes' category.
The approval lands **during the Commonwealth Games**, where India's team is having its best-ever medal haul.

depth.background: Khelo India is the Indian government's flagship scheme to develop grassroots sporting talent, built to create a structured pipeline of athletes from school competitions up through elite training centers, in response to India's historically modest medal counts at global multi-sport events relative to its population. Earlier iterations funded state-level competitions, sports infrastructure, and stipends for promising young athletes, but coaches and administrators have long argued the funding and athlete-identification numbers were too small to match India's ambitions. The **Union Cabinet**, chaired by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi**, has periodically extended and expanded the scheme, this time increasing its outlay again just as India's team delivers a record medal haul at the ongoing 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

stories.title: A wildfire flares back up in southern France, cutting off an entire village and forcing 2,500 more evacuations
stories.what_happened: A wildfire that firefighters believed they had contained earlier in the week reignited on July 31 south of the original burn area in the Var department of southeastern France, tearing through **1,000 hectares (about 2,470 acres) in just six hours**. The blaze forced the evacuation of roughly **2,500 people** near the Gros Bessillon massif, and completely cut off the village of Correns — home to about 1,000 people — because the fire made access roads impassable, leaving residents confined in place. A separate fire near Cotignac, also in Var, has burned 430 hectares since starting the same day. France deployed roughly **700 firefighters**, six water-dropping helicopters, eight Canadair water-bomber planes and two Dash aircraft to fight the flames, as a mistral wind and near-40°C heat fanned the embers. France's interior minister said wildfires have now scorched **115,000 hectares** nationwide so far this year.
key_points: The fire near **Correns** in the Var region destroyed **1,000 hectares in just six hours** after flaring up again.
**2,500 people** were evacuated near the Gros Bessillon massif; the **1,000-resident village of Correns** is cut off, with access roads impassable.
**700 firefighters**, six water-dropping helicopters, eight Canadair planes and two Dash aircraft are battling the blaze.
A **mistral wind** and temperatures near **40°C (104°F)** fanned the flames.
Wildfires have now burned **115,000 hectares** across France this year, per the interior minister.

depth.background: France has faced one of its worst wildfire years in recent memory, with blazes breaking out repeatedly through July across the south, including a major fire near Bordeaux that had already forced tens of thousands of evacuations earlier in the month. The **Var** department, a hilly, forested region in southeastern France near the Riviera, is especially fire-prone in summer heat, and this particular fire had reportedly been brought under control earlier in the week before flaring back up. Hot, dry **mistral winds** — which funnel down France's Rhône valley toward the Mediterranean — are a classic wildfire accelerant in the region, and this week's heat pushed temperatures close to 40°C.

stories.title: Modi's Cabinet extends India's biggest farmer cash-support scheme through 2031, at a cost of ₹3.15 lakh crore
stories.what_happened: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved continuing PM-KISAN for a further five years, from **2026-27 to 2030-31**, with a total financial outlay of **₹3.15 lakh crore**. The scheme pays ₹2,000 three times a year directly into farmers' bank accounts via DBT. Officials said more than **₹4.47 lakh crore** has already been transferred across 23 installments since the scheme began, and that internal studies show **85% of farmers** have cut back on borrowing because of the guaranteed payments. The Cabinet said continuing the scheme would help farmers invest in agriculture, improve productivity, reduce farming risk, and strengthen the rural economy.
key_points: The Union Cabinet approved continuing **PM-KISAN** from **2026-27 to 2030-31**, at a cost of **₹3.15 lakh crore** (roughly $38 billion).
Under the scheme, eligible farmers get **₹2,000 three times a year** (₹6,000/year), paid directly into their bank accounts.
Over **₹4.47 lakh crore** has been paid out across **23 installments** since the scheme launched in 2019.
The government says **85% of farmers** report borrowing less because of the guaranteed income support.

depth.background: **PM-KISAN** (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi) is a flagship Modi government scheme launched in 2019 that gives small and marginal farmers direct cash payments using **Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT)** — money sent straight to bank accounts rather than through subsidized inputs or middlemen. It is one of the largest direct cash-transfer programs to farmers anywhere in the world. The extension comes as rural income and farm distress remain a persistent political and economic issue in India.

stories.title: Bitcoin slides below $63,000 as hawkish Fed dissent and a stalled crypto bill spook traders
stories.what_happened: Bitcoin fell 2.9% to $62,929.27 as of 4:30pm ET Friday, with Ethereum down 2.8% to $1,866.57 and Solana down 2.0% to $73.04. The drop came as investors digested Wednesday's Fed meeting, where three regional presidents — Cleveland's Beth Hammack, Minneapolis's Neel Kashkari, and Dallas's Lorie Logan — dissented in favor of raising rates, a hawkish signal that made riskier assets like crypto less attractive. Coinbase and Strategy Inc. both posted results that disappointed Wall Street this week, adding pressure on crypto-linked stocks and sentiment. Growing doubt that lawmakers will pass the Clarity Act crypto legislation this summer further weighed on the market. Despite the Friday slide, Bitcoin was still positioned to close July roughly 7.5% higher for the month, aided by continued inflows into spot Bitcoin ETFs — including $233 million into such funds on Thursday alone, with BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust adding $183 million in assets.
key_points: Bitcoin fell **2.9% to $62,929** on Friday; Ethereum dropped 2.8% and Solana fell 2.0%.
Three Federal Reserve regional presidents **voted to raise rates** this week instead of holding — a hawkish surprise that hit risk assets.
Disappointing earnings from **Coinbase and Strategy Inc.** (formerly MicroStrategy) added to the pullback.
Doubts are growing that Congress will pass the **Clarity Act**, the crypto market-structure bill investors have been waiting on, before summer ends.
Despite Friday's drop, Bitcoin was still on pace to **end July up roughly 7.5%** for the month.

depth.background: Crypto prices move heavily on two things: how 'risky' investors feel overall, and US regulatory signals. The Federal Reserve had already surprised markets on July 29 when its policy meeting ended with **three regional bank presidents dissenting in favor of a rate hike** rather than holding steady — the first time since 2016 that three officials pushed the same direction at once, reflecting concern that inflation has stayed above the Fed's 2% target for **more than five years**. Separately, the crypto industry has been pushing Congress to pass the Clarity Act, a bill meant to spell out which US regulator oversees which digital assets — something the industry says it needs to attract more institutional money.

stories.title: Amazon stock jumps 12% on a blowout cloud quarter — while Apple sinks 8% the same week on a weak forecast
stories.what_happened: Amazon and Apple both reported quarterly results this week, and the market's reaction could not have been more different. Amazon's stock jumped roughly **12%** to around **$263** a share after AWS posted faster-than-expected revenue growth, powering a broader earnings beat. Apple's stock fell about **8%** to around **$308** a share **despite posting a record fiscal third-quarter revenue**, because its services division — the App Store, iCloud, subscriptions — grew slower than analysts expected, and the company's guidance for the next quarter disappointed investors. Microsoft and Meta also reported this week; Microsoft's results triggered the single biggest one-day market-value gain by any company in stock market history. Combined, Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft added close to **$1.5 trillion** in market value over the week.
key_points: Amazon shares surged about **12%**, adding roughly **$230 billion** in value in a day, after AWS cloud revenue grew faster than expected.
Apple stock fell about **8%** despite record quarterly revenue, dragged down by **weak services growth** and soft guidance.
Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft together added nearly **$1.5 trillion** in combined market value this week.
The split shows Wall Street is now judging Big Tech on whether **AI spending actually pays off**, not just on how much they spend.
Microsoft separately posted the **biggest single-day market-value gain in stock market history** this same earnings week.

depth.background: Big Tech's biggest companies — Apple, Amazon, Microsoft, Google (Alphabet) and Meta — have spent hundreds of billions of dollars building AI data centers and chips over the past two years. Investors mostly rewarded that spending on faith. Now, with quarterly earnings season underway, Wall Street is starting to demand **proof** that all that AI investment is generating real revenue, not just eating into profit margins. **AWS (Amazon Web Services)** is Amazon's cloud-computing division and its main profit engine, increasingly rented out to run other companies' AI workloads.

stories.title: Sensex and Nifty close higher for a third straight day, capping their best July in years
stories.what_happened: India's benchmark indices extended their winning streak on **Friday, July 31**, with the **BSE Sensex closing up 166.49 points (0.21%) at 78,094.64**, and the **Nifty 50 up 66.45 points (0.27%) at 24,383.60** — the third consecutive day of gains. Auto and financial-services stocks did the heavy lifting: Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Finserv and M&M were among the biggest boosts after their June-quarter results beat expectations. IT and FMCG stocks were the laggards, staying under pressure through the session. Zooming out, both indices notched their **second consecutive monthly gain in July**, up 2.1% (Sensex) and 2.2% (Nifty) for the month.
key_points: Sensex rose **166.49 points (+0.21%)** to close at **78,094.64**; Nifty gained **66.45 points (+0.27%)** to **24,383.60**.
It was the **third consecutive session** of gains for both benchmark indices.
**Auto and financial-services stocks led**, with Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Finserv and M&M boosted by strong June-quarter results.
**IT and FMCG stocks lagged** and dragged on the broader market.
For the month, Sensex and Nifty logged their **second straight monthly gain**, up **2.1% and 2.2%** respectively.

depth.background: Indian markets have been navigating cross-currents this month: **rising US bond yields have pressured the rupee**, and Trump's new 100% tariff on patented drugs has weighed on pharma sentiment, even as the broader macro backdrop stayed uncertain. Despite that, India's June-quarter (Q1FY27) corporate earnings season has been broadly supportive, particularly for consumer and financial names, while the **IT sector has lagged** on concerns about US client spending. The RBI has also been intervening heavily to defend the rupee this week.

stories.title: A hacker got DeepSeek to run cyberattacks almost by itself — because it had fewer safety brakes than Claude or ChatGPT
stories.what_happened: Palo Alto Networks' threat-intelligence unit, **Unit 42**, tracked a threat actor operating under the aliases knaithe and KnYuan, assessed to be based in **Zhuhai, China**. The attacker connected DeepSeek to an open-source agent framework called **Hermes Agent**, creating a pipeline that could scan for vulnerable internet-facing systems, choose which vulnerability to exploit, pull working exploit code from GitHub, and carry out the attack — all with just one initial instruction sent over Telegram. Over the course of the campaign, the system attempted to compromise more than **460 targets**, but only **three were successfully breached**: two involved stealing memory data from Citrix NetScaler devices, and one was a suspected session-hijacking attempt against a **Malaysian government entity**. Ironically, the operation was only discovered because the attacker's own tool exposed a public web server that leaked the operator's API keys, exploit scripts, and target lists — which is how Unit 42 got its detailed look inside.
key_points: Security firm **Unit 42** (Palo Alto Networks) uncovered a Chinese-speaking hacker using **DeepSeek** to run largely autonomous cyberattacks.
The attacker wired DeepSeek into an open-source tool called **Hermes Agent**, then controlled the whole operation with **a single Telegram message**.
DeepSeek then handled target-scanning, picking vulnerabilities, sourcing exploit code from GitHub, and launching attacks **with no further human input**.
Across roughly **460 attempted targets**, only **three were actually breached** — Unit 42 says the campaign was more proof-of-concept than mass success.
The hacker reportedly chose DeepSeek specifically because **Claude's and OpenAI's safety filters blocked** attempts to use them offensively.

depth.background: AI safety teams at companies like Anthropic and OpenAI build in guardrails that are supposed to refuse requests to help with hacking, malware, or other offensive cyber operations. Chinese AI lab **DeepSeek** has gained a reputation for being far more permissive, with weaker built-in refusals — attractive to legitimate researchers, but also to bad actors. Security researchers have warned for over a year that agentic AI — models that can act on their own toward a goal instead of just answering one question — would eventually be weaponized for autonomous hacking, and this is one of the clearest documented cases of it actually happening.

stories.title: Manipal Health's ₹8,000 crore IPO closes fully subscribed — but retail investors stayed cautious
stories.what_happened: Manipal Health Enterprises' initial public offering closed today, Friday, after being open for bidding since Wednesday, July 29. The price band was set at **₹560 to ₹590 per share**, and the fresh-issue portion aimed to raise about **₹8,000 crore**, alongside an offer-for-sale of existing shares worth roughly ₹1,275 crore. By the close, the issue was **fully subscribed**, driven mainly by qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) — big funds and banks — who bid **4.3 times** the shares set aside for them. Retail investors, however, were more hesitant, with subscription in that category running softer amid concerns the IPO's valuation is demanding. Share allotment is scheduled for **August 3**, with listing to follow shortly after.
key_points: The **Temasek-backed hospital chain's** IPO closed today after three days, priced at **₹560-₹590 per share**.
The issue was **fully subscribed**, with big institutional investors (QIBs) bidding **4.3 times** their allocated portion.
Retail investor demand was **softer**, reflecting concern the IPO is priced richly relative to the business.
The fresh-issue portion alone raised roughly **₹8,000 crore** (about $960 million).
Share allotment is expected **August 3**, ahead of a stock-market listing.

depth.background: Manipal Health Enterprises runs one of India's largest hospital chains and is backed by Singapore's sovereign wealth fund Temasek, a major global investor. India's hospital sector has drawn heavy investor interest in recent years as rising incomes and health awareness drive demand for private healthcare, and a wave of hospital-chain and healthcare IPOs (like Medanta-owner Global Health before it) have tested how much public investors are willing to pay for that growth. A **strong IPO market** overall in 2026 — with 114 IPOs completed in India by July — has made big-ticket listings like this one a barometer of investor risk appetite.

stories.title: F1 clears up confusion over Malaysia's returning Grand Prix — it will race in daylight, not under lights
stories.what_happened: The official F1 app briefly displayed an evening **8pm–10pm local** time slot for the Sepang-hosted race on October 4, sparking speculation on social media that it would be run as a night race under floodlights. Sepang International Circuit chief executive **Azhan Shafriman Hanif** clarified that the listing was an app error, and that the race will actually run in the **afternoon** local time. The race sits on the calendar between the Azerbaijan Grand Prix (September 26) and the Singapore Grand Prix (October 11), and marks Malaysia's return to the F1 calendar for the first time since 2017.
key_points: **Sepang International Circuit** confirmed the Malaysia-hosted **Bahrain Grand Prix** on **October 4** will run in the **afternoon**, not as a night race.
Confusion started after the official F1 app briefly listed an **8pm–10pm local** time slot, suggesting floodlit racing.
It's Malaysia's **first F1 race since 2017**, slotted between Azerbaijan (Sept 26) and Singapore (Oct 11).
The race keeps the **Bahrain Grand Prix** name even though it's being run at Sepang, not in Bahrain.

depth.background: Sepang hosted the Malaysian Grand Prix from 1999 to 2017 before F1 dropped it from the calendar. It's returning for 2026 as a substitute venue for a race still contractually branded the **Bahrain Grand Prix** — a scheduling quirk that has already caused confusion among fans. The addition comes amid a broader reshuffle of F1's calendar, including ongoing uncertainty over the season's Middle East races.

stories.title: Supreme Court strikes down Bihar rule that denied government jobs to married daughters of deceased employees
stories.what_happened: A Supreme Court bench of Justices **M.M. Sundresh** and **Prasanna B. Varale** ruled on **July 31** that Bihar's policy restricting compassionate appointments to divorced or deserted daughters — while imposing no equivalent restriction on sons — is unconstitutional. The Court held that **'any classification differentiating a daughter from a son is, per se, unconstitutional,'** and explicitly rejected the underlying assumption in the policy: **'There cannot be a presumption in law that, after marriage, a daughter severs her ties with her parental family.'** The ruling set aside the Patna High Court's earlier order upholding the rejection of the daughter's job claim, and directed the **State of Bihar to reconsider her compassionate-appointment claim on its merits within eight weeks**.
key_points: The Supreme Court ruled Bihar's policy limiting **compassionate appointments** to only divorced or deserted daughters is **unconstitutional**.
The bench held that treating daughters differently from sons after marriage violates **Article 14** — the right to equality.
The Court rejected the state's assumption that a married daughter **'severs ties'** with her parental family.
The ruling came in an appeal by **Sayara Khatoon** and her daughter, after Patna High Court upheld the job denial.
Bihar must now **reconsider the daughter's job claim on merits** within **eight weeks**.

depth.background: 'Compassionate appointment' schemes let Indian states give a government job to a family member of an employee who dies in service, so the family isn't left without income. Bihar's version of the scheme only allowed a daughter to be considered if she was divorced or deserted by her husband — treating a married daughter, in effect, as no longer part of her birth family, while placing no such condition on sons. Sayara Khatoon and her daughter challenged this after the daughter's claim was rejected following her father's death, and the Patna High Court had sided with the state.

stories.title: The Supreme Court ends Jammu & Kashmir CM Omar Abdullah's 17-year divorce battle, closing the case by mutual settlement
stories.what_happened: The Supreme Court, in a bench of Justices **PS Narasimha and Alok Aradhe**, granted a mutual-consent divorce to Omar Abdullah and Payal Abdullah, closing a legal battle that had run since he first sought dissolution of the marriage. The two had married on **September 1, 1994**, and lived separately since **2009**. After lower courts repeatedly rejected Abdullah's petition — a family court in 2016 and a Delhi High Court division bench in December 2023 — the Supreme Court referred the matter to its **Mediation Centre**, where the two sides worked out a complete settlement. Senior advocate **Kapil Sibal**, appearing for Abdullah, told the court the parties had resolved all outstanding issues and agreed to withdraw related proceedings, after which the bench disposed of the case.
key_points: The Supreme Court granted a **mutual-consent divorce** to Jammu & Kashmir Chief Minister **Omar Abdullah** and his estranged wife **Payal Abdullah**.
The couple married in **1994** and had been **living separately since 2009** — a legal fight that ran roughly **17 years**.
A family court had earlier **rejected** Abdullah's divorce petition, a ruling upheld by a Delhi High Court bench in **2023**.
The case was resolved after the Supreme Court referred it to **mediation**, where both sides reached a full settlement.
Senior advocate **Kapil Sibal** represented Abdullah; the bench included Justices **PS Narasimha** and **Alok Aradhe**.

depth.background: Omar Abdullah is the sitting Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir and a senior leader of the National Conference party, and the son of former Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Farooq Abdullah — one of the most prominent political families in the region. He married Payal Abdullah, who is of British-Sikh descent, in 1994, and the couple has been estranged and living separately since 2009, though the marriage was never formally dissolved for years despite Abdullah seeking it. A family court rejected his divorce petition in 2016 for failing to prove grounds like cruelty or desertion, and a Delhi High Court bench upheld that rejection in December 2023, pushing the matter to the Supreme Court.

stories.title: England leaves the door open for a 'stunning' Ben Stokes comeback ahead of next summer's Ashes
stories.what_happened: Rob Key, England's men's cricket managing director, said he would welcome a return from Ben Stokes to international cricket ahead of next summer's Ashes series against Australia, telling reporters **'anything is possible with Ben'** and that it would be a **'brilliant story'** if he did come back. Key's comments mark the first time a senior England official has publicly floated a Stokes U-turn since his shock mid-Test retirement roughly a month ago. Stokes stepped away from the England captaincy and international cricket entirely after England's 4-1 Ashes defeat in Australia, citing exhaustion. Key stopped short of confirming any concrete negotiations are underway, framing it as a door left open rather than an active recruitment effort.
key_points: England cricket chief **Rob Key** says he'd welcome Ben Stokes back before next year's **Ashes**.
Stokes shocked cricket by retiring from international cricket **a month ago**, mid-Test, after 15 years and 4 years as captain.
He said at the time he had **'burned himself out'** after England's **4-1 Ashes defeat** in Australia.
Key says **'anything is possible with Ben'** but stopped short of confirming any active talks.
A comeback would be a huge boost for England ahead of the next Ashes series against Australia.

depth.background: Ben Stokes is one of England's greatest modern cricketers — an all-rounder who captained the Test team for four years and famously led England to a World Cup win in 2019. He shocked English cricket a month ago by announcing his retirement from international cricket **mid-match**, during the fourth day of a Test decider against New Zealand, after 15 years and 4 years as Test captain, at age 35. He said he no longer had 'any fight left' after England's 4-1 Ashes series defeat in Australia and had started contemplating retirement even earlier, during a difficult run that included being dropped for a nightclub incident. **Rob Key** is England men's cricket managing director, the top administrator responsible for team selection and strategy.

stories.title: F1 boss Stefano Domenicali says fans 'don't care' about telemetry graphics — and viewers are furious
stories.what_happened: At a press briefing, Domenicali said fans are **'not interested'** in technical details like throttle angle or brake pressure during overtakes, adding **'nobody cares how drivers are driving the car.'** He pointed to a conversation with filmmaker George Lucas in Hungary as evidence, saying viewers are drawn to the drama and action rather than the mechanics behind it. The comments followed weeks of fan complaints that F1's broadcasts at races including **Silverstone and Spa-Francorchamps** dropped on-screen telemetry graphics — data on battery deployment, speed, and braking that had previously helped viewers understand how an overtake actually happened. Supercars driver **Scott Pye** publicly accused Domenicali of 'insulting fans' for dismissing their interest in the data. The row comes just as F1 shuts down for its mandatory two-week summer break, giving it time to simmer without fresh on-track news to displace it.
key_points: Domenicali said **'no one is interested'** in throttle, brake, or driving-style data.
F1 broadcasts at **Silverstone and Spa** dropped battery, speed, and braking graphics entirely.
A Supercars driver accused Domenicali of **'insulting fans'** who want to understand overtakes.
Domenicali cited a chat with filmmaker **George Lucas** about what excites viewers.
The row lands right as F1 enters its **two-week summer break**.

depth.background: Formula 1 has spent the last several seasons trying to make its TV product more accessible to new fans, adding graphics that show real-time data like brake pressure, throttle position, and battery deployment during overtakes. Under CEO **Stefano Domenicali**, who has led F1's commercial growth since 2021, the sport has generally leaned into more data and storytelling for casual viewers, following the model set by Drive to Survive. That's what makes his recent comments — playing down fan interest in exactly that kind of data — land as a surprising reversal to longtime viewers.

stories.title: Apple falls 7%, Amazon jumps 12% after earnings — Wall Street is now picking AI 'winners and losers'
stories.what_happened: Apple and Amazon both reported quarterly earnings this week, and investors reacted in opposite directions. Apple's results **beat expectations** on revenue and per-share profit, but the company guided to **9–11% revenue growth** next quarter, below the roughly 12% analysts wanted, blaming **supply-chain constraints**. Its shares fell about **7%**. Amazon, by contrast, raised its planned 2026 capital spending to roughly **$220 billion** — up from a prior $200 billion estimate — mostly to keep building AI data-center capacity, and its stock still jumped about **12%**, because its cloud unit AWS showed strong enough growth to make that spending look justified rather than wasteful.
key_points: **Apple** beat on revenue and profit but fell **~7%** after warning of weaker guidance, citing **supply constraints**.
**Amazon** surged **~12%** even after raising its 2026 AI-infrastructure spending plan to about **$220 billion**, up from $200 billion.
The split: Amazon's cloud arm **AWS** grew fast enough to justify that spending; Apple's guidance suggested it isn't spending big on AI capacity at all.
Apple's iPhone and services revenue actually **topped estimates** — the stock fall was about the outlook, not the results themselves.
Investors who treated Apple as a **'safe' non-AI-spender** are now reconsidering, given Amazon and Microsoft's stronger numbers.

depth.background: Since 2023, the biggest US tech companies have been locked in a massive spending race on **AI infrastructure** — data centers, chips, and cloud capacity — betting that AI demand will keep growing fast enough to justify it. Investors have been split on whether this spending is smart growth or a bubble. Apple has mostly stayed out of that race, instead leaning on its iPhone/services business and using AI features built on partners' models rather than building its own giant data centers.

stories.title: A wildfire firefighters thought they'd beaten reignites in southern France, forcing 2,500 people to flee
stories.what_happened: On the afternoon of **Friday, July 31**, the previously-contained Gros Bessillon fire flared back up around 1:30pm as violent mistral winds swept through the region, and within hours it had burned through another **1,250 hectares** of land. That's on top of the **4,500 hectares** the same fire had already consumed the week before, bringing the total scorched area to roughly **5,750 hectares**. Var prefect Simon Babre ordered the evacuation of **2,500 people** from the villages of Correns, Montfort-sur-Argens, Carcès, Le Val and Châteauvert, saying the fire was "moving faster than a horse at a gallop." By August 1, the emergency response had grown to more than **1,300 firefighters**, backed by 8 Canadair water-bombing planes, 2 Dash aircraft and 6 helicopters. As of the morning of August 1, French authorities said containment lines were holding and no new areas had burned overnight, though the situation remained classified as active, not resolved.
key_points: The **Gros Bessillon fire** in France's Var region, declared under control just three days earlier, **reignited around 1:30pm on July 31** in violent mistral winds.
It burned through another **1,250 hectares**, on top of **4,500 hectares** the same fire had already destroyed the week before — nearly **5,750 hectares** total, close to the size of Paris.
**2,500 residents** were evacuated from five villages: Correns, Montfort-sur-Argens, Carcès, Le Val and Châteauvert.
**1,300+ firefighters**, 8 Canadair water-bomber planes, 2 Dash aircraft and 6 helicopters were mobilized to hold the containment lines.
Temperatures in the Var hit **around 40°C (104°F)**, part of the same summer heat wave fueling simultaneous major wildfires in Greece and Spain.

depth.background: The **Var department**, in France's Provence region near the Riviera, has been one of the hardest-hit spots in Europe's 2026 wildfire season, with this same area already burning multiple times since mid-July. Southern France regularly deals with the **mistral** — a strong, dry, cold wind that funnels down the Rhône valley and can turn a small brush fire into a fast-moving inferno within hours. This summer has combined that wind pattern with a prolonged heat wave and drought across the Mediterranean, drying out vegetation until it becomes effectively kindling. French authorities had marked the Gros Bessillon fire as "fixed" (contained) only three days before it broke out again.

stories.title: Trump's 100% tariff on patented drugs takes effect today — but Pfizer, Eli Lilly and the rest of Big Pharma won't actually pay it
stories.what_happened: Today, July 31, was the deadline written into April's proclamation for the tariff to start hitting the 17 pharmaceutical companies specifically named in its Annex III. In practice, nothing changes for any of them: all 17, a list that includes Pfizer, Eli Lilly, and Novo Nordisk, have already signed MFN pricing agreements and had onshoring plans approved, which under the same proclamation earns them a **0% tariff rate through January 20, 2029**. Trade press covering the deadline described it as tariffs 'with no one left to kick' — the mechanism worked as an incentive, not as a tax that actually collects revenue from anyone. The broader 100% tariff still looms for every other patented-drug importer that hasn't struck a deal, with that deadline pushed to September 29, 2026.
key_points: A **100% tariff** on patented pharmaceutical imports officially takes effect today for **17 major drugmakers** named in April's order.
None of them will pay it: all 17 — including **Pfizer, Eli Lilly, and Novo Nordisk** — struck **'Most-Favored-Nation' (MFN)** pricing deals with Washington first.
Companies with a signed MFN deal and an approved US 'onshoring' plan get a **0% tariff until January 2029** instead.
Generic drugs, US-made products, and rare-disease treatments are **exempted entirely** from the tariff.
Everyone else — smaller and foreign drugmakers without a deal — still faces the **100% rate starting September 29**.

depth.background: In April 2026, President Trump signed a proclamation imposing a 100% 'Section 232' tariff — a national-security-justified import tax — on patented drugs and the ingredients used to make them, arguing the US relies too heavily on foreign-made medicines. To soften the blow, the administration invited major pharmaceutical companies to sign 'Most-Favored-Nation' pricing agreements, promising to charge the US no more than other wealthy countries pay for the same drugs, in exchange for tariff relief and a pledge to build more manufacturing in the US ('onshoring'). Since then, most of the industry's biggest names have taken that deal rather than risk the tariff.

stories.title: Parliament shuts down for the weekend as Opposition uproar over the July 20 crackdown boils over
stories.what_happened: Both Houses of Parliament were adjourned for the day on **July 31** amid continued sloganeering by Opposition MPs, with the Chair announcing the Houses would not reconvene until **Monday, August 3 at 11 am**. In the Lok Sabha, opposition members disrupted proceedings but the House still managed to pass the **Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026** without any debate. The Rajya Sabha was separately adjourned amid uproar over multiple issues, chiefly the alleged **police action against student protesters on July 20**. Opposition MPs gathered at Makar Dwar, a key protest spot within the Parliament complex, holding placards and demanding Home Minister Amit Shah respond directly to their questions about the crackdown.
key_points: Both the **Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha** were adjourned for the day amid Opposition sloganeering, with proceedings not resuming until **Monday, August 3**.
Opposition MPs from **INDIA bloc parties** protested at Makar Dwar, demanding Home Minister **Amit Shah** answer for police action during the July 20 student march.
Despite the disruption, the Lok Sabha still passed the **Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, 2026** — without debate.
This is part of a pattern this Monsoon Session: bills are getting passed with minimal discussion while the Opposition's core grievance goes unaddressed.
The protest ties back to a police crackdown on students demonstrating over the **NEET paper-leak issue** on July 20.

depth.background: India's **Monsoon Session of Parliament** runs from July 20 to August 13, 2026, and has been repeatedly disrupted since a police crackdown on student protesters on its opening day. Those students were demonstrating over alleged **NEET (National Eligibility cum Entrance Test) paper leaks**, a recurring flashpoint in Indian politics because NEET determines medical college admissions for hundreds of thousands of students. The **INDIA bloc** — the main opposition coalition — has since used nearly every sitting to demand accountability from the government over how that protest was handled, repeatedly stalling normal legislative business.

stories.title: Union Cabinet clears ₹84,084 crore 'Samudra Manthan' scheme to hunt for oil and gas deep under the ocean
stories.what_happened: The **Union Cabinet**, chaired by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi**, approved the petroleum ministry's **'Samudra Manthan' National Offshore Exploration Scheme**, a Central Sector Scheme with a total outlay of **₹84,084 crore** to be spent through **FY 2030-31**. The scheme is designed to de-risk deepwater and ultra-deepwater oil and gas exploration by reimbursing companies for up to half the cost of exploratory wells and part of the cost of 3D seismic surveys, making it commercially viable to search for hydrocarbons in India's harder-to-reach offshore basins. Those basins — off India's eastern and western coasts, in waters as deep as 3,000 metres — are estimated to hold more than **5,600 MMTOE** of hydrocarbon potential. State explorer **ONGC** has already begun drilling its first deepwater well under the mission, in the **Mahanadi basin**, and could spend as much as **$20 billion** over five years hiring specialized deepwater drillships and rigs as part of the broader push.
key_points: India's **Union Cabinet** approved the **'Samudra Manthan' National Offshore Exploration Scheme** with an outlay of **₹84,084 crore** (about **$10 billion**).
The scheme runs through **FY 2030-31** and aims to reduce the **financial risk** of deepwater and ultra-deepwater drilling for private and global energy firms.
Under the framework, the government will reimburse **up to 50% of exploratory well costs** and part of the cost of 3D seismic surveys.
India's offshore basins are estimated to hold more than **5,600 million tonnes of oil equivalent (MMTOE)** of hydrocarbon potential, in waters up to **3,000 metres deep**.
State-run **ONGC** may spend up to **$20 billion** hiring deepwater rigs over a five-year exploration push under the same mission.

depth.background: India currently imports roughly **85% of the crude oil** it consumes, making it heavily exposed to global oil-price swings and supply shocks — a vulnerability that became especially visible this week as oil jumped past **$92 a barrel** on the widening Iran conflict. Deepwater exploration is far more expensive and riskier than shallow-water drilling, which has historically discouraged both Indian and foreign energy companies from fully exploring India's offshore basins. 'Samudra Manthan' — named after a Hindu mythological churning of the ocean that yields great treasures — is the government's answer: a state-backed scheme to absorb some of that financial risk so companies actually drill.

stories.title: Pakistan face a series-defining second Test against West Indies in Trinidad after Shan Masood's injury blow
stories.what_happened: Pakistan lost the first Test of their two-match series against West Indies by **90 runs** at Tarouba, despite a **century from Shan Masood**; chasing 211 in the fourth innings, Pakistan collapsed to be bowled out for just **120**, with Seales taking **5/20**. Masood, Pakistan's best batter in the match, has since been **ruled out of the second Test** with a fractured finger sustained batting through pain in that innings. With the series already lost 1-0, Pakistan must win the second Test, starting **August 2 at Queen's Park Oval, Port of Spain**, just to draw the series — and they'll do it without their in-form captain.
key_points: **West Indies lead the two-match series 1-0** after a **90-run win** in the first Test at Tarouba.
Pakistan will be without in-form opener and captain **Shan Masood**, ruled out with a **fractured finger** after scoring a century in the first Test.
The second Test starts **August 2** at **Queen's Park Oval, Port of Spain** — Pakistan's last chance to level the series.
West Indies' pace attack — **Jayden Seales, Justin Greaves and Shamar Joseph** — routed Pakistan's batting, with Seales taking **5 wickets for 20 runs** in the second innings.

depth.background: Pakistan have historically struggled in **Caribbean conditions**, where fast, bouncy pitches favor genuine pace bowling, and this tour is part of the ongoing **World Test Championship** cycle, where series results earn points toward a place in the WTC final. West Indies' pace-heavy attack has been in good recent form, while Pakistan's batting — outside of captain Shan Masood — has looked fragile.

stories.title: Bangladesh name a pace-depleted squad for their first-ever Test tour of Australia
stories.what_happened: The Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) announced a 15-member squad for a historic two-Test tour of Australia, running from **August 13–17 in Darwin** and **August 22–26 in Mackay**. The squad includes uncapped fast bowler **Musfik Hasan**, handed his first senior call-up after a string of injuries hit Bangladesh's pace attack — most notably ruling out lead strike bowler **Nahid Rana**. With those absences, not a single player in the touring squad has previous experience playing a Test match in Australian conditions, making this a significant gamble against a team that has historically dominated at home.
key_points: Bangladesh will tour Australia for **two Tests** in August 2026 — their **first trip there in 23 years**
Uncapped fast bowler **Musfik Hasan** has been called into the 15-member squad
Strike bowler **Nahid Rana** is among several pace bowlers unavailable through injury
The Tests run **Darwin (Aug 13–17)** and **Mackay (Aug 22–26)** — Australia's first home winter Tests since 2004
**No player** in the squad has ever played a Test on Australian soil before

depth.background: Bangladesh has played Test cricket since 2000 but has never before toured Australia, one of the sport's toughest away assignments because of its fast, bouncy pitches that suit express pace bowling. Australia usually hosts its home Tests in the Southern Hemisphere summer around Christmas and New Year, but this series is scheduled for the Australian winter — the first time Australia has hosted home Tests in that season since 2004 — as cricket boards experiment with the international calendar.

stories.title: IPL 2027's first big trade is official: Rishabh Pant returns to Delhi Capitals, Kuldeep Yadav moves to Lucknow
stories.what_happened: Delhi Capitals and Lucknow Super Giants confirmed a direct player swap: **Rishabh Pant** rejoins Delhi Capitals, taking a pay cut to a revised **₹15 crore** fee from the ₹27 crore LSG originally paid for him, while **Kuldeep Yadav** heads to Lucknow at his existing **₹13.5 crore** valuation. It marks Pant's return to the franchise where he made 111 appearances across nine seasons from 2016-2024, the most of any player in Delhi Capitals' history. The trade is the first major, officially completed swap of the IPL 2027 trade window, which opened in late June and stays open into December ahead of the mini-auction.
key_points: **Delhi Capitals and Lucknow Super Giants** have officially completed a high-profile player swap.
**Rishabh Pant** returns to Delhi Capitals at a revised fee of **₹15 crore**, down from the ₹27 crore LSG paid in the 2025 mega auction.
**Kuldeep Yadav** moves to Lucknow Super Giants at his existing fee of **₹13.5 crore**.
Pant played **9 seasons and 111 matches** for Delhi Capitals (2016-2024) before this, more than any other player in the franchise's history.
It's the **first confirmed trade** of the IPL 2027 window, which stays open until around December.

depth.background: The IPL introduced a mid-season and off-season **trade window** allowing franchises to swap contracted players outside the annual auction, and the window for IPL 2027 opened in late June 2026. Pant had spent nearly a decade as Delhi Capitals' marquee wicketkeeper-batter before moving to Lucknow Super Giants in the 2025 mega auction; Kuldeep Yadav, a left-arm wrist-spinner, had built a five-season career at Delhi Capitals taking 72 wickets in 65 matches before also being auctioned away. This trade effectively reverses both moves at once.

stories.title: Toto Wolff vows he 'will not allow' a Hamilton-Rosberg-style rivalry to fester between George Russell and Kimi Antonelli
stories.what_happened: Speaking to RacingNews365 as F1 entered its summer break, Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff addressed the risk of a repeat of the Hamilton-Rosberg rivalry now that both his 2026 drivers are fighting for the championship. Asked directly if he could see history repeating, Wolff said: 'I will not allow it. That's never going to happen to me again... I'm just taking a driver out if he does that.' The comment is a notably blunt threat — effectively saying he would remove a driver from the team rather than let a title fight curdle into open conflict. It follows Antonelli's rise to championship leader through the first half of the 2026 season, a surprise given Russell's greater experience, and comes as the pair head into F1's mandatory two-week factory shutdown with the title fight still to resolve.
key_points: Mercedes boss **Toto Wolff** says he'd rather **drop a driver outright** than let internal rivalry turn toxic again.
The comparison is to **Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg**, Mercedes teammates whose feud famously boiled over in the mid-2010s.
**Kimi Antonelli** currently leads the 2026 drivers' championship, with teammate **George Russell** also in title contention.
Wolff told reporters: **'I will not allow it... I'm just taking a driver out if he does that.'**
The remarks land as both drivers head into F1's mandatory **summer break** with the title fight still open.

depth.background: Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg were Mercedes teammates from 2013 to 2016, and their rivalry — which began friendly and turned openly hostile, including on-track collisions between them — is remembered as one of the most damaging teammate conflicts in modern F1. Wolff ran Mercedes throughout that era and has spoken before about wanting to avoid a repeat. Now, with rookie sensation Kimi Antonelli leading the championship and experienced teammate George Russell also a contender, the same dynamic — two teammates fighting for one title — is emerging again.

stories.title: Imesha Dulani's maiden century powers Sri Lanka Women past Pakistan in T20I series opener
stories.what_happened: Chasing a target of **177** at the **Rangiri Dambulla International Stadium**, Sri Lanka Women got off to a flying start as **Athapaththu** smashed **39 off 22 balls** with five fours and two sixes, before **Imesha Dulani** took over and anchored the chase with an unbeaten **101 off 64 balls**, hitting 17 fours and a six. Sri Lanka reached **177-4** with six balls remaining to complete a six-wicket win. For Pakistan, **Shawaal Zulfiqar** scored a maiden Women's T20I half-century, but it came in a losing cause. The win puts Sri Lanka **1-0 up** in the three-match series.
key_points: **Imesha Dulani** scored an unbeaten **101 off 64 balls** as Sri Lanka Women chased down **177** to beat Pakistan Women by **six wickets** in the first T20I at Dambulla.
Dulani becomes only the **second Sri Lankan cricketer ever** — after **Chamari Athapaththu** — to score a century in a Women's T20I.
She got early support from captain **Chamari Athapaththu**, who blazed **39 off 22 balls** with five fours and two sixes.
Sri Lanka reached **177-4** with **six balls to spare**, chasing one of the highest totals in the format.
Pakistan's **Shawaal Zulfiqar** scored a maiden WT20I half-century, but it wasn't enough as Sri Lanka took a **1-0 lead** in the three-match series.

depth.background: Sri Lanka and Pakistan's women's teams are contesting a **three-match T20I series**, part of a busy 2026 international calendar for both sides. **Chamari Athapaththu**, Sri Lanka's captain and one of the format's most destructive batters, had previously been the only Sri Lankan woman to score a Women's T20I century — a record Dulani now shares, marking a breakthrough moment for a Sri Lankan batting order that has often relied heavily on Athapaththu alone.

stories.title: Ashwin names his India squad for the 2027 World Cup — backs Bhuvneshwar Kumar's return, drops Pant and Samson
stories.what_happened: Ashwin named his projected 15-player India squad for the 2027 ODI World Cup, built around captain **Shubman Gill**, with **Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli** both included as they continue playing ODI cricket after retiring from Tests and T20Is. His most eye-catching call was backing a recall for **36-year-old pacer Bhuvneshwar Kumar**, who hasn't played for India in any format since 2022. His most surprising omissions were **wicketkeeper-batters Rishabh Pant and Sanju Samson**, both currently established India players. In the spin department, Ashwin picked **Kuldeep Yadav** as the team's main spin option ahead of Washington Sundar. His full batting and bowling picks included Shreyas Iyer, KL Rahul, Ishan Kishan, Axar Patel, Hardik Pandya, Harshit Rana, Mohammed Siraj and Jasprit Bumrah.
key_points: Former India spinner **Ravichandran Ashwin** picked his 15-man squad for the **2027 ODI World Cup**.
He wants veteran pacer **Bhuvneshwar Kumar** recalled despite not playing for India since **2022**.
**Rishabh Pant and Sanju Samson** were his most surprising omissions from the squad.
Ashwin picked **Kuldeep Yadav** over Washington Sundar as the team's main spinner.
**Shubman Gill** was named captain, with Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli both included.

depth.background: The 2027 ODI Cricket World Cup will be held across **South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia**. Ravichandran Ashwin, one of India's greatest spin bowlers with over 500 Test wickets, retired from international cricket and now works as a cricket commentator and analyst, regularly sharing his views on India's team selection. Bhuvneshwar Kumar, now 36, was a key part of India's white-ball bowling attack for years but has not played for India since **2022** due to fitness concerns and the team management moving on to younger pace options.

stories.title: Lando Norris says he felt 'violated' after a 40-minute paparazzi car chase through London
stories.what_happened: Lando Norris said a paparazzi photographer tailed his car for 40 minutes as he drove across London to visit a friend's house, waiting to see who he'd meet and where he'd go. Speaking as he entered the F1 summer break, Norris said the experience left him feeling 'violated' and that he's had to change his private-life habits — including skipping dinners out — specifically to avoid being photographed. He said he accepts scrutiny as part of being a Formula 1 driver and reigning world champion, but drew a firm line against being physically followed. Norris is spending the break with friends and family, saying he plans to play golf and padel to work on his fitness ahead of next month's Dutch Grand Prix.
key_points: F1 **world champion Lando Norris** said he felt **'violated'** after being followed by a paparazzi photographer for **40 minutes** while driving through London to meet a friend.
Norris said it **'doesn't feel as though private life is private'** anymore, and that he now avoids going out to dinner to escape being photographed.
He drew a clear line: he'll accept media attention as part of being an F1 driver, but **'there are boundaries, and I won't accept people following me.'**
The comments came as Norris started his **F1 summer break**, which he's spending with friends and family, playing golf and padel.
The incident adds to a broader, recurring tension between elite athletes and loss of privacy as their fame grows — Norris is F1's reigning world champion.

depth.background: Formula 1's mandatory summer shutdown runs for two weeks every year in late July/August, when teams are barred from working on their cars and drivers get a rare real break from the 24-race season. As F1's global popularity has grown — driven partly by Netflix's 'Drive to Survive' — its top drivers have become mainstream celebrities well beyond motorsport fans, bringing the kind of tabloid and paparazzi attention usually reserved for film or music stars.

stories.title: Tens of thousands of migrants storm Spain's Ceuta enclave from Morocco, at least 18 dead
stories.what_happened: Over roughly 24 hours, an estimated **60,000 people** crossed from Morocco into Ceuta — most by swimming around the Tarajal breakwater or wading along the shoreline, overwhelming the checkpoint. **At least 18 people died**, drowned or killed in a crush near the barrier, though some outlets report higher tolls; the exact number is still being confirmed. The sudden arrival — equivalent to **70% of Ceuta's population** in a single day — swamped local reception facilities, and Ceuta's government asked Madrid to declare a national emergency. Spain's interior ministry said most who crossed have already returned to Morocco voluntarily, and blamed migrant-smuggling networks for exploiting the recent Supreme Court ruling to organize the surge.
key_points: **~60,000 migrants** crossed from Morocco into Spain's tiny Ceuta enclave in a single 24-hour surge — equal to **70% of the city's population**.
At least **18 people died**, some drowning near the Tarajal breakwater and others crushed in a stampede; some reports put the toll far higher.
Most who crossed **returned to Morocco voluntarily within hours**, after the sheer numbers overwhelmed Ceuta's reception centers and triggered a humanitarian emergency.
Ceuta's local government has asked Madrid to **declare a national emergency**.
The surge followed a **Spanish Supreme Court ruling** blocking fast-track deportations of migrants intercepted trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla by sea — a ruling smugglers are accused of exploiting.

depth.background: Ceuta is one of two small Spanish territories on the coast of North Africa (the other is Melilla) — technically part of the **European Union**, even though they sit on the African mainland next to Morocco. That makes them one of the only land borders between Africa and the EU, and a longstanding pressure point for migration, with people trying to reach them by climbing fences, swimming, or crossing by sea. Spain and Morocco jointly police the border, and **Morocco's cooperation has historically been the main thing keeping crossings in check** — leverage Rabat has used in disputes with Madrid before. A recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling curbed the fast-track deportation procedure Spain used against people caught reaching these enclaves by sea.

stories.title: Verstappen tells Red Bull to 'find more performance' as the only top-4 team yet to win in 2026
stories.what_happened: Speaking as the season heads into its summer break, Verstappen said Red Bull can't ease off and **'need to find more performance,'** specifically citing ongoing issues with the RB22's balance and unresolved 'anomalies' with the current package. Red Bull remains the only team among the championship's top four that hasn't won a race in 2026, even though Verstappen has picked up **five podium finishes**. He said the team is improving but urged caution, describing the approach as **'one race at a time.'** The comments follow a season in which Red Bull has repeatedly acknowledged it started 2026's new rules era behind its main rivals.
key_points: Verstappen said Red Bull **'need to find more performance'** heading into the second half of the season.
Red Bull is the **only team inside the top four** that hasn't won a grand prix so far in 2026.
Verstappen has taken **five podiums** this year but no wins, and sits down in the drivers' standings.
He specifically flagged the car's **reliability and setup 'anomalies'**, not just outright pace.
The comments come as F1 enters its **summer break** before the Belgian Grand Prix weekend.

depth.background: Red Bull won four consecutive drivers' championships with Verstappen from 2021-2024, making them the dominant force in F1. But **2026's all-new technical rules** (a major regulation reset covering engines and aerodynamics) reshuffled the competitive order, and Red Bull has struggled to match rivals like McLaren, Ferrari and Mercedes so far this season. Verstappen has been openly critical of his car, the **RB22**, throughout the year, including a well-publicized 'told you so' moment after a setup disagreement at the Canadian Grand Prix in May.

stories.title: Lewis Hamilton shuts down the theory that 2026's new rules just happen to suit his driving style
stories.what_happened: Speaking ahead of F1's summer break, Lewis Hamilton **rejected the idea** that the 2026 regulation changes are simply more suited to his driving style than to other drivers'. He said he hasn't had to change his approach more than usual to adapt to the new cars. The comments come after a season in which Hamilton has scored **169 points** with **five podiums in six races**, including his **first Grand Prix win for Ferrari**, in Barcelona — a sharp contrast to a winless, podium-less 2025.
key_points: Hamilton says the **2026 regulations** aren't inherently 'more rewarding' for his style, pushing back on a common fan/media theory.
He's had his **best season with Ferrari** since joining — **169 points**, five podiums in six races, and his **first win for the team**, at Barcelona.
2025, his first Ferrari season, was reportedly the **worst of his career** — no podiums at all.
The turnaround has fueled speculation the new car rules simply favor how Hamilton naturally drives, which he's now directly disputed.
The comments come heading into F1's **summer break**, a natural moment for reflection on the season so far.

depth.background: Formula 1 introduced a **major regulation overhaul for the 2026 season** — new car designs, power units and rules — which resets the competitive order and changes how much a driver's individual style matters versus the car itself. Lewis Hamilton, a seven-time world champion, moved to **Ferrari** for 2025 and endured what's been called the worst season of his career, failing to reach a single podium. His marked improvement in 2026 has led some to argue the new rules simply favor his particular driving technique, rather than reflecting genuine gains from him or the team.

stories.title: Congo's Ebola outbreak surges to the second-largest on record — and the fastest-growing ever
stories.what_happened: The **World Health Organization** confirmed the DRC's Ebola outbreak has grown to **3,360 confirmed cases and 1,487 deaths** as of data through July 27, with **98 new cases** reported in the most recent update — the vast majority from Ituri province. Health officials say the outbreak is spreading faster than any Ebola outbreak in history, reaching in a matter of weeks case counts that took years to accumulate in past epidemics. **733 people are currently hospitalized** in isolation as health teams work to contain the virus. The outbreak, which began in mid-May 2026, has now surpassed most historical Ebola outbreaks in scale and is being described by health officials as spreading "like wildfire."
key_points: The Ebola outbreak in the **Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)** has topped **3,360 confirmed cases** and **1,487 deaths** as of the latest WHO data (through July 27).
It is now the **second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded**, and cases have piled up **faster than in any previous outbreak**, taking just weeks to reach levels that took years before.
**733 patients** are currently hospitalized in isolation units.
The **98 newest cases** came mostly from Ituri province (**87 cases**), with North Kivu (11 cases) also affected.
The outbreak began in **mid-May 2026** and has already killed more people than most Ebola outbreaks in history.

depth.background: **Ebola** is a severe, often fatal viral hemorrhagic fever first identified in the DRC in 1976, spread through contact with bodily fluids of infected people or animals. The DRC has battled more Ebola outbreaks than any other country, including a 2018–2020 outbreak in the east that killed over 2,200 people and was, until now, one of the worst on record. This current outbreak, concentrated in the conflict-affected **Ituri and North Kivu provinces**, is complicated by ongoing armed conflict in the region, which makes it harder for health workers to trace contacts and vaccinate at-risk populations.

stories.title: Japan's Kumamoto earthquake death toll climbs to 34 as rescuers enter a fourth day searching a collapsed mall
stories.what_happened: The magnitude 7.1 quake hit Kumamoto Prefecture on Tuesday, July 28, and roughly 80 minutes later an explosion tore through the Aeon Mall in the town of Kashima — a complex with about 200 stores — collapsing part of its second floor and trapping workers inside. At least **7 of the 34 confirmed deaths** are tied to that mall explosion; the mall's operator has not ruled out a gas leak as the cause. Separately, **8 people died** at a Nippon Paper Industries mill in Yatsushiro. As of Friday, July 31, rescuers had confirmed **129 injuries** and roughly **10,000 people displaced**, many sheltering in summer heat. Search-and-rescue crews are now four days into the operation, and authorities still don't have a firm count of how many people remain unaccounted for.
key_points: A **magnitude 7.1 earthquake** struck Kumamoto Prefecture on Japan's Kyushu island on Tuesday, July 28.

The death toll has climbed to **34**, including at least **7 people killed when part of the Aeon Mall's second floor collapsed** after an explosion about 80 minutes after the quake — officials haven't ruled out a gas leak.
**8 more people died** at a Nippon Paper Industries mill in Yatsushiro, hit by the same quake.
Roughly **129 people were injured** and about **10,000 people have been displaced**, sheltering through a summer heatwave.
Rescue operations are now in their **fourth day**, and officials still don't know how many people remain missing.

depth.background: Kyushu, Japan's third-largest island, sits on the boundary of several tectonic plates and has a history of destructive earthquakes — including a pair of major quakes that hit this same Kumamoto region in April 2016. Japan enforces some of the strictest building codes in the world specifically because of this earthquake risk, which is why a secondary building collapse — like the one at the Aeon Mall — gets investigated as its own disaster rather than treated as ordinary quake damage.

stories.title: Japan's Kumamoto earthquake death toll climbs to 34 as search enters day 4 amid dangerous heat
stories.what_happened: Japan's Kumamoto prefectural government said Friday that the earthquake death toll has climbed to **34**. Seven of the deaths came from an explosion that brought down a shopping mall in the town of Kashima, and eight more people died at a paper mill in Yatsushiro. Search-and-rescue operations entered their **fourth day** on Friday, with officials still unsure how many people remain missing or the full scale of home damage across the region. Rescue crews are now also contending with **36°C (97°F) heat**, adding a health risk on top of the physical danger of unstable rubble.
key_points: The death toll from Tuesday's **magnitude 7.1 earthquake** in Kyushu has risen to **34**.
At least **seven died** when the quake triggered an **explosion at a shopping mall** in Kashima.
**Eight more died** at a Nippon Paper Industries mill in Yatsushiro.
Search operations are now in their **4th day**, with the number still missing unclear.
Rescuers face **36°C heat** in Kumamoto, raising fears of heat illness among survivors and crews.

depth.background: A magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck Japan's southern island of Kyushu on Tuesday, July 28, toppling a factory chimney, flattening homes, and triggering a deadly explosion at a shopping mall. Kyushu is home to several million people, and Kumamoto prefecture has a history of destructive quakes, including a major one in 2016. Japan's building codes and disaster response are among the world's most advanced, yet the mall explosion and mill collapse show how quickly secondary disasters can add to a quake's toll.

stories.title: China's factories unexpectedly shrink in July, snapping the recovery Beijing was counting on
stories.what_happened: China's National Bureau of Statistics reported that its official manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) — a monthly survey asking factory managers whether output, orders, and hiring are rising or falling — dropped to **49.2 in July**, down from 50.3 in June. A reading above 50 signals expansion; below 50 signals contraction, so this is the sector shrinking for the first time since February. The miss was driven by a slump in domestic orders and **typhoons disrupting production and logistics** in coastal manufacturing regions. Part of the earlier strength had come from exporters front-loading shipments ahead of anticipated US tariffs, and economists say that boost is now unwinding. The data came one day after China's Politburo publicly called for more supportive, incremental economic policy to keep growth on track into the final years of the current Five-Year Plan.
key_points: The official factory gauge (PMI) fell to **49.2** in July from 50.3 in June — any number below 50 means activity is shrinking.
It's China's **first manufacturing contraction since February**, and missed economists' forecast of a flat 50.0.
Typhoons disrupted production and **domestic orders slumped** as an earlier export rush ('front-loading' ahead of tariffs) faded.
It lands a day after China's top leadership **pledged more economic support**, underlining why they felt the need to act.
The **IMF had just raised** its 2026 China growth forecast to 4.6% — this data cuts against that optimism.

depth.background: China's economy has spent 2026 trying to shake off a slowdown driven by weak consumer spending, a still-fragile property sector, and on-and-off US tariff pressure. Factories had been propped up partly by companies **rushing to ship goods** before new tariffs could bite — a pattern economists call 'front-loading.' On July 30, the **Political Bureau of the Communist Party's Central Committee** met and called for stronger domestic demand and 'timely, practical' stimulus, a signal Beijing knew growth was fragile even before this data landed.

stories.title: Russia's third straight night of strikes kills more Ukrainians, and a missile crossing into Poland forces NATO jets into the air
stories.what_happened: On the night of July 30 into July 31, Russia launched one of its largest barrages of the war so far — more than **70 missiles and 280 drones** — hitting Kyiv, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Cherkasy, Lviv and Dnipropetrovsk regions and killing at least **10 civilians**, including a family of six (four of them children) in a single house near Kryvyi Rih. A Russian **Kh-101 cruise missile** strayed into **Polish airspace** and crashed; Poland scrambled Polish F-16 fighter jets, a NATO refueling aircraft and an early-warning plane in response, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the missile was likely not aimed at Poland but that his forces were ready to shoot it down had it continued toward a populated area. Attacks continued into July 31, killing at least **9 more people** and injuring **48**, as Russia deployed roughly **255 additional Shahed-type drones** overnight. Ukrainian officials said the sustained barrage aims to grind down air defenses and energy infrastructure ahead of autumn.
key_points: Russian strikes killed at least **9 more people** and injured **48** across Ukraine on July 31 — the third mass-strike night in a row.
Russia fired **255 Shahed-type drones** overnight, part of a barrage that has topped **70 missiles and 280 drones** since July 30.
A suspected Russian **Kh-101 missile** crossed into **Polish airspace** and crashed, triggering a NATO jet scramble.
Poland's PM said forces were **prepared to shoot it down** had it kept heading toward a populated area.
The strikes come **days after** a missile killed **six members of one family**, including four children, in Dnipropetrovsk.

depth.background: Russia has escalated long-range missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent weeks, even as intermittent diplomatic contacts continue elsewhere in the war. **Poland**, a NATO member bordering Ukraine, has repeatedly found Russian drones and missile debris landing or flying through its airspace during these barrages — a recurring flashpoint because NATO's founding treaty commits all **32 members** to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelensky has used these incidents to press Western allies for more air-defense systems. Deadly strikes on Ukrainian population centers that occasionally clip Poland's edges have become one of the most closely watched signs of how close the war could come to directly drawing in NATO.

thread.previously: We reported a Russian missile killed six members of one family, including four children, in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region as part of a mass overnight strike.
thread.changed: The barrage extended into a third night, killing at least 9 more people and injuring 48 across Ukraine, while a separate Russian missile crossed into Polish airspace and forced NATO to scramble jets — a new escalation dimension beyond the original strike.
