stories.title: F1 heads to Spa for the Belgian Grand Prix, where battery management could matter more than horsepower
stories.what_happened: Formula 1's 2026 season moves to **Spa-Francorchamps** for the Belgian Grand Prix, Round 10, a little over two weeks after the British Grand Prix at Silverstone. Teams and drivers face what officials are calling an **"energy-poor" circuit** — Spa's long flat-out sections mean cars must carefully balance harvesting and deploying battery power under the new 2026 hybrid rules, and getting that wrong could cost more time than a bad qualifying lap. **Ferrari** goes into the weekend with real momentum, having won two of its last three races, while **Mercedes** arrives under pressure to recapture the early-season form that once made it a title contender, all while its two drivers continue to push each other hard internally. The Ardennes region's famously changeable weather adds another layer of unpredictability, with the threat of scattered rain capable of scrambling strategy calls for any team.
key_points: The **Belgian Grand Prix** is Round 10 of the 2026 season, held at **Spa-Francorchamps**, the longest lap on the calendar.
It's the first standard-format race weekend since the dramatic **British Grand Prix** at Silverstone.
**Energy management**, not just raw pace, is expected to decide the race under F1's new 2026 hybrid power units.
**Ferrari** arrives with momentum, having won **two of its last three races**.
**Mercedes'** internal driver battle keeps intensifying heading into the weekend.

depth.background: 2026 introduced a new generation of F1 hybrid power units that lean much more heavily on electrical energy than before, which makes circuits with long **full-throttle sections** — like Spa's famous straights — especially demanding, since cars can run low on stored battery power before a lap is done. Spa-Francorchamps, tucked into Belgium's Ardennes forest, is one of the most historic and longest circuits on the calendar, known for unpredictable weather that can turn a race on its head. Round 10 arrives with the season's competitive order still shifting: Ferrari has picked up form recently, while Mercedes has had a rockier stretch despite entering the year as an early favorite.

stories.title: RBI sells dollars for a third straight day to defend the rupee near its record low
stories.what_happened: The rupee hurtled toward its all-time low of **96.96 per dollar** last week as Middle East tensions spiked oil prices and global investors favored the dollar. Bankers estimate the RBI sold **$8 billion to $9 billion** across spot and forward markets on Friday alone to defend the currency, then followed up with further dollar sales on Monday and Tuesday -- a third consecutive day of intervention, deliberately timed around off-peak trading hours to get more impact per dollar spent. That sustained selling triggered stop-loss unwinding among traders who had bet on further rupee weakness, accelerating the currency's recovery. Combined with crude oil prices easing on hopes of a US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough, the rupee is now expected to hold above the 96/dollar level at Tuesday's market open, a level it had been in danger of breaching entirely.
key_points: The rupee weakened toward its **record low of 96.96 per dollar** last week as Middle East tensions pushed up oil prices.
The RBI reportedly sold an estimated **$8-9 billion** on Friday alone, according to bankers.
The central bank has now intervened for a **third straight day**, targeting off-peak trading hours to amplify its impact.
Softening **crude oil prices**, on hopes of a US-Iran deal, are also helping take pressure off the currency.
The rupee is expected to **hold above the 96/dollar mark** at Tuesday's open.

depth.background: India imports roughly **90% of the oil** it uses, so a weaker rupee makes fuel, and everything that depends on it, more expensive -- which is why the central bank cares so much about defending psychologically important levels like 97 to the dollar. The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** manages currency swings mainly by buying or selling dollars from its foreign-exchange reserves; heavy selling like this week's is a costly, limited tool, not something it can do indefinitely. The current pressure traces back to escalating Middle East tension around the Iran war, which pushed oil prices up and rattled global currency markets, compounded by elevated US Treasury yields pulling investment money toward the dollar.

stories.title: A magnitude-7.1 earthquake in Japan's chip-making heartland kills 18 and halts Sony and Tokyo Electron plants
stories.what_happened: A **magnitude-7.1 earthquake** struck Kumamoto Prefecture on Japan's southern island of Kyushu on **Tuesday, July 28, at 07:27 UTC** (4:27pm local time), with a shallow epicenter about 10km deep near Kumamoto City, home to roughly 700,000 people. The quake cut power to thousands of homes, cracked roads, and triggered a tsunami warning that was later lifted. A chimney collapse at a Nippon Paper Industries factory killed five workers, and a shopping mall partially caved in as rescuers searched for survivors. By **July 29, the confirmed death toll had climbed to 18**, with at least 62 people injured, and officials warned the number could keep rising. Chipmakers reacted immediately: **Sony and Renesas paused production** with no restart date given, Tokyo Electron suspended two of its Kumamoto factories, and Honda idled a nearby motorcycle plant, while TSMC said its own site was largely undamaged and resumed operations quickly.
key_points: A **magnitude-7.1** quake hit Kyushu, Japan's chip hub, on **July 28**
At least **18 people killed**, 62+ injured, toll still rising
**Sony and Renesas paused chip production**; Tokyo Electron shut two factories
The region makes camera sensors for the **iPhone** and equipment used by chipmakers worldwide
TSMC's nearby fab was largely undamaged and back running quickly

depth.background: Kyushu, in southern Japan, is one of the most important semiconductor manufacturing regions on Earth — home to TSMC's newest Japan factory, Sony's image-sensor plants (which supply camera sensors for the iPhone and most premium smartphones), chipmaker Renesas, and **Tokyo Electron**, a company that builds much of the specialized machinery used to make chips everywhere. Japan sits on some of the world's most active fault lines and suffered a similarly damaging earthquake sequence in this same city, Kumamoto, back in 2016. Rescue crews are still combing through rubble, including a collapsed factory chimney and a partially collapsed shopping mall.

stories.title: Magnitude-7.1 earthquake hits southern Japan, mall collapse leaves at least 9 dead and 250 injured
stories.what_happened: A shallow **magnitude-7.1 earthquake** (Japan's Meteorological Agency measurement; the US Geological Survey initially logged 7.1 before revising toward 6.8) struck Kyushu at **4:27pm local time** on Tuesday, hitting the maximum **Shindo 7** intensity level in the hardest-hit areas. In Kashima Town, the second floor of an **Aeon Mall shopping center** collapsed, trapping an unknown number of shoppers and staff; fire officials said around **20 to 30 employees** were initially unaccounted for, with several people already pulled from the rubble and taken to hospital. Elsewhere in the Kumamoto region, the quake sparked several fires, damaged bridges, derailed a cargo train, and left a number of houses at risk of toppling over. A tsunami advisory covering the nearby Ariake and Yatsushiro Seas was issued and then lifted about two hours later after only minor sea-level changes were recorded. Japanese authorities have not yet given a final damage assessment, and rescue operations at the collapsed mall were still underway as of this report.
key_points: A **magnitude-7.1 earthquake** struck Kyushu, Japan's southern main island, at **4:27pm local time** on Tuesday.
The quake registered the highest level, **Shindo 7**, on Japan's shaking-intensity scale.
The second floor of an **Aeon Mall shopping center** in Kashima Town, Kumamoto, collapsed, trapping dozens of people.
At least **9 people have died** and **more than 250 are injured** so far, with rescue crews still searching the mall.
A tsunami advisory was issued for nearby coasts and **lifted within two hours**, with no major tsunami detected.

depth.background: Japan sits directly on the Pacific 'Ring of Fire,' a horseshoe-shaped belt of fault lines that makes it one of the most earthquake-prone countries on Earth, with strict building codes built around that reality. Kyushu, the island hit today, has a painful precedent: a pair of earthquakes in **2016** centered on Kumamoto killed **273 people** and reshaped how Japan thinks about aftershock risk in this exact region. Kumamoto is also a major hub for **advanced semiconductor manufacturing** -- Sony and TSMC both operate large chip plants there -- which is why an earthquake in this specific area draws global industrial attention, not just humanitarian concern.

stories.title: Deep depression makes landfall near Haldia, triggering red alerts and evacuations across Odisha-Bengal
stories.what_happened: The deep depression crossed the West Bengal-north Odisha coast near Haldia, between Baleshwar and Canning, on the morning of July 28, bringing intense rainfall, strong winds and rough seas. The IMD issued a red warning — its highest alert level — for extremely heavy rainfall in Sundargarh, Kendujhar and Mayurbhanj districts, and flagged ten Odisha districts overall, including Balasore, Bhadrak, Cuttack, Jagatsinghpur, Jajpur, Puri and Khordha, as likely to see heavy to extremely heavy rain. Odisha's Revenue and Disaster Management Minister directed all district administrations to stay on round-the-clock alert, ensure timely evacuation of people in vulnerable low-lying or riverside areas, and arrange food, drinking water and shelter for those displaced. Fishermen were told to avoid the northwest Bay of Bengal and the Odisha-Bengal-north Andhra coast until the morning of July 29.
key_points: The deep depression crossed the **West Bengal-north Odisha coast near Haldia** on the morning of July 28.
IMD issued a **red warning** for extremely heavy rain in **Sundargarh, Kendujhar and Mayurbhanj** districts.
Ten Odisha districts, including **Balasore, Cuttack and Puri**, are on alert for heavy to extremely heavy rainfall.
Odisha's government ordered **24×7 monitoring** and timely evacuation of people in vulnerable areas.
Fishermen are told to **stay off the northwest Bay of Bengal** until the morning of July 29.

depth.background: A 'deep depression' is a stage of a tropical weather system — stronger than an ordinary low-pressure area but not yet strong enough to be classified a cyclone — that still carries heavy rain and strong winds. The Bay of Bengal regularly spins up these systems during India's June-to-September monsoon, and Odisha and West Bengal's low-lying, densely populated coastal districts are especially exposed to flooding when one makes landfall. The IMD had already flagged this system as a risk over the weekend, prompting early school closures.

thread.previously: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) had put Odisha and West Bengal on red alert for a deep depression forming over the Bay of Bengal, forcing school closures in three districts.
thread.changed: The depression has now actually crossed the coast near Haldia, and red warnings for extremely heavy rain have widened to more districts as evacuation orders go out.

stories.title: Israel and Lebanon set next round of Rome talks for August 4–6, building on their first troop pullout
stories.what_happened: US officials confirmed that Israeli and Lebanese delegations will hold their next round of talks in Rome from **August 4 to 6**, at the same US Embassy venue used for prior rounds. The agenda: expand the pilot-zone model to more territory, resolve lingering border disputes, and move toward fuller implementation of the framework deal. A State Department official said the two sides are approaching the talks with **'significant momentum'**, citing the smooth handover of the first pilot zones and Lebanese President Joseph Aoun's meeting with President Trump last week. Even so, Israel's defense minister has told the Pentagon that Israeli troops will remain **indefinitely** in the broader security zones it holds across Lebanon, Syria, and Gaza — meaning full withdrawal is not imminent.
key_points: The **next round of US-mediated talks** is set for **Rome, August 4–6**, a State Department official confirmed.
Talks will cover **expanding the pilot zone** in southern Lebanon and settling **border disputes**.
It follows the **successful launch of the first pilot zone**, where Lebanese Army troops replaced Israeli soldiers.
The push builds on the **14-point framework agreement** signed in Washington on **June 26**, which calls for Hezbollah's disarmament.
Lebanese President Aoun met Trump last week, which US officials called a source of **'significant momentum'**.

depth.background: Israel and Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militant group that controls much of southern Lebanon, fought an intense war in 2024 that devastated the border region. A **US-brokered framework deal** signed on **June 26, 2026** laid out a path to end the conflict for good: Hezbollah disarms, and Israeli troops leave in stages as the **Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF)** take over security. Since then, negotiators have met repeatedly in Rome to iron out the mechanics, focusing first on two small **'pilot zones'** north and south of the Litani River where the LAF has now taken over from Israeli soldiers as a proof of concept.

stories.title: Meta apologises after PM Modi's Facebook video is briefly pulled down, Centre summons company's global leadership
stories.what_happened: A **selfie-style video** Prime Minister Narendra Modi posted on Facebook on **July 23**, addressing Gen Z during the ongoing student protests, was found to have been **removed** from the platform. Meta acknowledged the removal and called it a **'technical glitch,'** with a spokesperson saying: **'The content was removed in error and has since been restored.'** India's **Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)** said it is taking the incident **'seriously'** and has summoned Meta and Instagram's **global leadership** to explain what happened. The episode surfaced even as Modi's Instagram following passed **105 million**, underlining how closely his government tracks his reach on Meta's platforms.
key_points: A **3-minute Facebook video** of PM Modi addressing Gen Z was **removed**, then restored within hours.
Meta called it a **'technical error'** and said the content was **'removed in error and has since been restored.'**
India's **IT Ministry (MeitY)** has summoned **Meta and Instagram's global leadership** over the incident.
The video was posted **July 23**, during the **36-day student protest** led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).
It comes as Modi's Instagram following just crossed **105 million**.

depth.background: Indian authorities have grown increasingly assertive about how global tech platforms handle political content, and government summons of Meta or X executives over content decisions are now a recurring feature of India's tech-policy landscape. The removed video was part of PM Modi's direct outreach to young Indians during weeks of student unrest over the **NEET exam-leak protests** led by the Cockroach Janta Party, making its disappearance — even briefly — politically sensitive at a moment when the government is trying to manage that unrest. Meta has previously apologized for similar content-moderation errors involving other governments' leaders.

stories.title: Parliament strikes a deal to actually debate the anti-paper-leak bill, easing the NEET-crackdown standoff
stories.what_happened: After repeated adjournments this week over the opposition's protest against the July 20 crackdown, the government and opposition reached an agreement to hold a substantial, extended debate — reported at eight to ten hours — on the **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026**, which had already been introduced in the Lok Sabha. The bill would toughen penalties for exam paper leaks and related malpractice, raising the maximum jail term to 10 years and fines up to ₹10 crore. Congress leader **Rahul Gandhi** is expected to speak during the debate, giving the opposition a high-profile platform to raise its concerns about both the bill and the police crackdown. Rather than rushing the bill to a vote today, both sides agreed to the longer discussion format, effectively de-escalating — at least temporarily — the standoff that had repeatedly halted proceedings.
key_points: The government and opposition agreed to an **extended 8-to-10-hour debate** on the **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026**.
**Rahul Gandhi** is set to speak on the bill, marking the opposition's most prominent voice entering the debate directly.
The bill proposes raising penalties for **paper-leak offences** to up to **10 years in jail and a ₹10 crore fine**.
It comes after days of deadlock over the **July 20 police crackdown** on NEET protesters at Jantar Mantar.
Both sides chose a **full debate over passing the bill immediately**, allowing extended scrutiny rather than a rushed vote.

depth.background: India's original Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act was passed in 2024 after repeated exam paper leaks disrupted competitive exams like NEET (the national medical-entrance test) for millions of students. A fresh 2026 paper-leak and CBSE on-screen-marking scandal reignited nationwide protests, including a sit-in at Delhi's Jantar Mantar that drew a police crackdown on July 20 — an event the opposition has used to stall Parliament's Monsoon Session for days, demanding accountability from Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. That standoff even bled into the unrelated hunger strike by activist Sonam Wangchuk, whose fast over the same paper-leak issue ended only after the government agreed to his demands.

thread.previously: We reported Parliament was adjourned again this morning as the opposition pushed its protest over the July 20 police crackdown on NEET protesters into a fight over a new anti-paper-leak bill, deepening the deadlock in the Monsoon Session.
thread.changed: Rather than staying stuck, the government and opposition reached an agreement today for an extended eight-to-ten-hour debate on the bill, with Rahul Gandhi set to speak — a concrete step out of the standoff rather than another adjournment.

stories.title: Parliament is adjourned again as opposition presses the NEET-crackdown showdown into a new bill fight
stories.what_happened: Today's session opened straight into disruption, with both houses gaveled shut amid heavy sloganeering before resuming later in the morning. The government used the session to formally introduce the **Public Examinations Amendment Bill, 2026**, which amends the existing 2024 anti-cheating law with seven new provisions: prison terms of **up to 10 years**, fines of **up to ₹10 crore**, confiscation of a guilty party's assets, and the power for states to set up fast-track special courts so cases are resolved within three months rather than dragging for years. Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju urged all parties to actually debate the bill's substance. But opposition MPs, including from Congress and regional parties, are using the four-hour debate slot to keep the spotlight on the police response to the July 20 march rather than the bill's text — arguing accountability for the crackdown matters as much as new penalties for future leaks.
key_points: Both the **Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha were adjourned** today amid renewed opposition sloganeering, continuing yesterday's showdown.
The flashpoint bill this week is the **Public Examinations Amendment Bill, 2026**, meant to toughen penalties for exam paper leaks.
The bill proposes **up to 10 years in prison, fines up to ₹10 crore**, asset confiscation, and fast-track special courts for offenders.
The government has scheduled a **4-hour debate** with young NDA MPs including Bansuri Swaraj and Tejasvi Surya leading the case for it.
Opposition MPs are using the bill debate to keep pressing on the **July 20 police crackdown** on NEET paper-leak protesters, not just the bill's contents.

depth.background: India's Monsoon Session of Parliament, which began July 20, has been dominated by fallout from the NEET-UG 2026 exam paper leak scandal. A youth-led protest movement (the 'Cockroach Janta Party') demanded the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, culminating in a massive Jantar Mantar-to-Parliament march on July 20 that was met with a police lathi-charge (baton charge) and tear gas. Pradhan ultimately resigned on July 25 after a 26-day hunger strike by activist Sonam Wangchuk and government assurances on protester amnesty — but the opposition has kept the political pressure on over how the protest itself was policed, forcing repeated adjournments this week (see yesterday's coverage).

thread.previously: Yesterday, the opposition forced a showdown in Parliament specifically over the July 20 police crackdown on NEET protesters, disrupting proceedings.
thread.changed: Today the fight has attached itself to a concrete piece of legislation — the Public Examinations Amendment Bill — with the government trying to steer debate toward the bill's tough new penalties while the opposition keeps redirecting it back to crackdown accountability, and both houses were adjourned again as a result.

stories.title: The Fed's two-day meeting starts today — traders now think a rate hold is more likely than a cut
stories.what_happened: The Fed's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) — the group of officials who set US interest rates — began its scheduled two-day meeting today, with the rate decision due tomorrow, July 29. Going into the meeting, futures markets (where traders bet on what the Fed will do) put the odds of a **hold at rates unchanged around 64%**, a sharp shift from just a week earlier when a hold looked far more certain at 87%. That shift reflects genuine uncertainty: inflation is running hot, with the Consumer Price Index up **4.2% year-over-year through May 2026** — the sharpest annual rise since April 2023 — which normally argues for the Fed to keep rates high or even raise them. But there are also signs of a softening labor market pulling in the opposite direction, toward a cut. The rate has held at **3.50%-3.75%** since the last change, and Warsh's shift away from forward guidance means officials aren't tipping their hand before Wednesday.
key_points: The **Federal Reserve's policy meeting runs July 28-29**, with a decision due Wednesday.
Markets now price roughly a **64% chance the Fed holds rates steady**, down sharply from an 87% chance just a week ago.
The Fed's target range has sat at **3.50%-3.75%** since its last move.
New Fed Chair **Kevin Warsh** has already changed how the Fed communicates — dropping traditional forward guidance for a **pure 'data-dependent' approach**, making each meeting harder to predict.
US inflation (CPI) rose **4.2% over the year to May 2026**, the biggest 12-month jump since April 2023 — well above the Fed's usual 2% comfort zone.

depth.background: The Federal Reserve is the US central bank — it sets the short-term interest rate that ripples through mortgages, credit cards, business loans, and, because the US dollar and Treasury market are the anchor of global finance, borrowing costs worldwide including in India. Earlier this year the Fed brought in a new chair, Kevin Warsh, who has shifted the Fed's style: instead of pre-signaling what it plans to do next ("forward guidance"), the Fed now says it will decide meeting-by-meeting based purely on incoming data. That makes each Fed decision, including this one, more of a genuine toss-up for markets than it used to be.

stories.title: Supreme Court calls the ₹8 lakh income cap for EWS quota 'prima facie reasonable'
stories.what_happened: A bench of **Justice PS Narasimha and Justice Alok Aradhe** on July 28 orally remarked that the ₹8 lakh income limit for EWS reservation is prima facie reasonable, while hearing petitions originally filed in 2021 challenging the National Testing Agency's use of a 27% OBC and 10% EWS quota in NEET's All India Quota for medical college admissions. The case traces back to the Supreme Court's January 2022 ruling, which upheld the EWS and OBC quotas for that year's admissions but said the validity of the ₹8 lakh criterion itself would be decided later. The government has told the court it intends to retain the ₹8 lakh norm. The bench also moved to consolidate several similar pending petitions so they can be heard together rather than piecemeal.
key_points: A bench said the **₹8 lakh annual family income** cutoff for EWS reservation looks reasonable, for now
The remark came while hearing **petitions filed in 2021** challenging NEET's EWS and OBC quota rules
It is only an **oral, provisional observation** — the final written verdict is still pending
The court is working to **consolidate overlapping petitions** that challenge the same income limit
The EWS quota reserves **10% of seats** for economically weaker sections outside caste-based categories

depth.background: India's **EWS (Economically Weaker Sections) quota** was introduced in 2019 as a 10% reservation for financially disadvantaged applicants who don't qualify for existing SC/ST/OBC reservations. The Supreme Court upheld the quota itself in January 2022, but explicitly left the ₹8 lakh income-eligibility threshold — recommended by a government-appointed committee — open to later challenge. Petitioners have long argued the figure is **arbitrary**, partly because it mirrors the separate 'creamy layer' income limit used to exclude better-off OBC applicants, even though EWS and OBC families face very different circumstances.

stories.title: India's Commonwealth Games medal count hits 10 after an all-night session in Glasgow
stories.what_happened: India's medal count at the Commonwealth Games 2026 climbed to **10 overall** (two gold, five silver, three bronze) after an eventful overnight session in Glasgow. **Weightlifting remains India's strongest suit**, contributing six of the ten medals so far. On the track, **Sarvesh Kushare won silver in the men's high jump final**, while weightlifters and para-athletes added further medals across multiple weight categories. Tuesday's schedule (Day 5) is headlined by **Gulveer Singh**, the national 10,000m record holder and Asian champion, competing in a direct final for his first-ever Commonwealth Games podium finish. India's boxing squad also has **five fighters in quarter-final bouts**, each already guaranteed a shot at a semi-final spot and at least a bronze medal if they win.
key_points: India's medal tally **doubles to 10** (2 gold, 5 silver, 3 bronze) by Day 5
**Weightlifting has delivered 6 of India's 10 medals** so far
Sarvesh Kushare wins **silver in the men's high jump final**
Gulveer Singh, the national record holder, runs the **men's 10,000m final** today chasing a first CWG podium
Five Indian boxers reach **quarter-finals**, each guaranteed at least a shot at bronze if they advance

depth.background: The Commonwealth Games 2026 are being held in Glasgow, and India has fielded a large contingent across athletics, weightlifting, boxing, swimming and more. India's campaign opened with a high-jump storyline (Kushare vs Tejaswin) and built momentum through Mirabai Chanu's opening weightlifting gold and a run of medals from the weightlifting team. Sharmila Dhankar's para-athletics gold on Day 4 was historic, ending a 20-year wait for an Indian medal in that discipline at the Games.

thread.previously: On Day 4, India closed with 5 medals total, headlined by Sharmila Dhankar's historic para-athletics gold in the women's shot put F57 -- India's first Commonwealth Games para-athletics medal in 20 years.
thread.changed: By the end of Day 5's overnight session, India's medal count has doubled to 10 -- two gold, five silver, three bronze -- with weightlifting alone contributing six of them, and Sarvesh Kushare adding a high-jump silver.

stories.title: Zelensky's 30,000-more-troops claim meets Seoul's skepticism as North Korea's war role deepens
stories.what_happened: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia is preparing to receive **30,000 additional North Korean troops**, with preparations under way since June in Russia's Voronezh region, close to the Ukrainian border. If it happens, this would **almost triple** North Korea's troop commitment beyond the roughly 14,000 currently believed to be serving with Russian forces. Zelensky added that Russia is also readying new North Korean ballistic missile launchers. South Korean government sources, however, say they are only tracking the reports and have **no confirmed evidence** yet that a new deployment is under way -- a notable gap between Kyiv's warning and Seoul's official caution.
key_points: Zelensky says Russia is preparing space for **30,000 more North Korean troops** in its Voronezh region
That would **roughly triple** North Korea's current troop contribution to the war
**South Korea's own government** says it has no confirmed signs of a new deployment yet
Zelensky also says Russia is preparing to receive new **North Korean ballistic missile launchers**

depth.background: North Korea has backed Russia's war on Ukraine since 2024, when it first sent thousands of troops to help Russia retake territory in its own Kursk region after a surprise Ukrainian incursion. Around **14,000-20,000 North Korean soldiers**, including special forces and combat engineers, have been deployed to Russia so far, alongside artillery shells and missiles. In return, Pyongyang has reportedly gained battlefield experience for its army and technological help from Moscow. South Korea, the US and their allies see the arrangement as a serious escalation because it ties two adversaries closer together militarily.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's claim that Russia was trying to bring in another 30,000 North Korean troops for the Ukraine war, on top of the roughly 14,000-20,000 already deployed since 2024.
thread.changed: Today, South Korean government sources say they are watching the reports closely but have found no confirmed signs of a new deployment yet -- an official note of caution on Zelensky's claim -- while new reporting adds that Russia is also preparing to receive new North Korean ballistic missile launchers.

stories.title: Desert Vipers Thrash San Francisco Unicorns by 9 Wickets in Global Super League
stories.what_happened: San Francisco Unicorns won the toss, batted first, and could only post 151 for 7 in their 20 overs. In reply, Desert Vipers made light work of the chase, racing to 152 for 1 in just 16.1 overs to win by nine wickets with 23 balls unused. Zachary Carter led the chase with a rapid 55 off 29 balls and also chipped in with the ball, taking 1 for 9, earning him the Player of the Match award.
key_points: **San Francisco Unicorns** were held to **151/7** batting first at Providence Stadium in Guyana
**Desert Vipers** chased the target down for the loss of just **one wicket**, finishing on **152/1 in 16.1 overs**
West Indies all-rounder **Zachary Carter** starred with an unbeaten-paced **55 off 29 balls** plus **1/9** with the ball to win Player of the Match
It was **Match 7** of the 2026 Global Super League, a five-team T20 tournament running **July 23 to August 1**
The dominant win strengthens Desert Vipers' position as the competition heads into its final week before the August 1 final

depth.background: The Global Super League is a T20 franchise tournament now in its third edition, bringing together five club sides from different countries and leagues — Desert Vipers (UAE's ILT20), Lahore Qalandars (Pakistan Super League), Perth Scorchers (Australia's Big Bash), Guyana Amazon Warriors (Caribbean Premier League) and San Francisco Unicorns (USA's Major League Cricket) — to play a round-robin plus playoffs, all hosted at Providence Stadium in Guyana. Desert Vipers, champions of the UAE's ILT20 in 2026, came into this match looking to build on an already useful position in the group table.

stories.title: West Indies rip through 14 wickets in a single day to seize control of the Trinidad Test
stories.what_happened: Day 3 turned into one of the most eventful days of Test cricket this year, with **14 wickets falling across both innings** in a single session-packed day. West Indies seamer **Justin Greaves** ran through Pakistan's lower order with a career-best five-wicket haul, helping bowl Pakistan out cheaply in their second innings. But Pakistan's own bowlers, **Abbas and Ali**, struck back hard when West Indies batted again, cutting through the top order and giving themselves a real chance at a comeback win. Late in the day, an unbeaten **33-run partnership between Kemar Roach and Shamar Joseph** steadied West Indies and pushed their overall lead past 150 runs, closing the day at a **155-run lead** with wickets still in hand.
key_points: **14 wickets fell** on Day 3 of the West Indies-Pakistan 1st Test at Tarouba — an unusually violent day of cricket.
West Indies' **Justin Greaves took a career-best five-wicket haul** to tear through Pakistan's lower order.
Pakistan struck back too, with **Abbas and Ali** taking wickets to cut into the West Indies innings.
An unbeaten **33-run stand between Kemar Roach and Shamar Joseph** pushed West Indies' lead past 150.
West Indies ended Day 3 with a lead of **155 runs**, putting them firmly in control heading into Day 4.

depth.background: This is the first Test of Pakistan's tour of the West Indies, being played at the Brian Lara Stadium in Tarouba, Trinidad, from July 25-29. Pakistan had already given up a slim first-innings advantage after West Indies bowled them out for 282, with Shan Masood's gritty century not enough to prevent a 29-run deficit (covered here yesterday) — a story that turned dramatically today.

thread.previously: Yesterday, Shan Masood's century wasn't enough to stop West Indies bowling Pakistan out for 282, leaving West Indies with a slim 29-run first-innings lead.
thread.changed: Today that slim lead exploded into a commanding one: 14 wickets fell in a single day, Justin Greaves took a career-best five-for, and West Indies closed Day 3 leading by 155 runs with wickets in hand.

stories.title: AI Spending Fears Trigger Kospi Circuit Breaker as Samsung, SK Hynix Crash
stories.what_happened: On Tuesday, July 28, investors dumped Korean chip stocks the moment markets opened, sending the Kospi down more than 8% and forcing Korea Exchange to freeze all trading for 20 minutes at 10:13:43 a.m. — the third circuit breaker this month alone. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which together make up a huge share of the index's value, led the rout, both falling by double digits at their worst point. The Kosdaq saw an identical plunge and matching halt. The selloff had been building since Monday, when SanDisk, Micron and Western Digital all sank on Wall Street over the same worry: that hyperscalers' (the giant cloud companies like Microsoft, Google and Meta) massive AI data-center spending is running ahead of any proven payoff, and that CXMT's blockbuster IPO signals Chinese competitors can now undercut Korean and US memory makers on price. SK Hynix was due to report its second-quarter earnings the same day, adding extra volatility around the stock.
key_points: South Korea's benchmark **Kospi** index plunged more than **8%** at the open, forcing the exchange to trigger a marketwide **circuit breaker** (an automatic 20-minute trading halt) at **10:13 a.m.** local time — the **8th** such halt in 2026 and the **14th** ever.
**Samsung Electronics** fell as much as **9.5–10%** and **SK Hynix** dropped up to **11–13%**, making them the two biggest losers in the entire **MSCI Asia Pacific** index, which fell about **3%**.
The **Kosdaq** (Korea's smaller-cap tech exchange) also fell over **8%** and triggered its own separate circuit breaker.
SK Hynix's US-listed shares had already closed overnight at **$143.02**, below their **$149** IPO price, after SanDisk sank **12%** and Micron dropped **5%** on Wall Street the prior session.

The panic followed China's memory-chip maker **CXMT** going public a day earlier and soaring as much as **530%**, becoming the world's 4th-largest DRAM maker and reviving fears it can undercut Samsung and SK Hynix on price.

depth.background: Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix together control roughly **65%** of the world's DRAM (computer memory chip) market, and their stocks have soared through 2026 on a wave of investment tied to the artificial intelligence boom — chips like theirs go into the servers that power AI systems like ChatGPT and Gemini. That rally has made Korea's Kospi index a global bellwether for whether investors still believe AI spending will pay off. China's CXMT, a state-linked memory maker, is racing to catch up and just listed its shares in Shanghai on July 27, instantly becoming China's most valuable listed company and stoking fears it will flood the market with cheaper chips.

stories.title: Samsung and SK Hynix post record AI-chip profits — but their stocks crash anyway
stories.what_happened: SK Hynix, the world's second-largest memory-chip maker and a key Nvidia supplier, reported **record Q2 2026 operating profit of roughly $41.6 billion**, a **557% jump** from a year earlier, and record net profit of about $64.1 billion. Despite this, the stock fell **9.6%** — a record one-day drop for its US-listed shares — because the results still **missed Wall Street's higher expectations** (analysts had forecast ₩64 trillion in operating profit; SK Hynix delivered ₩60.54 trillion) and management gave no details on shareholder returns. A day later, Samsung Electronics forecast its own quarterly operating profit would jump roughly **19-fold** from a year ago, again on booming AI memory demand, and said the industry-wide chip crunch would persist **until 2028**. The mismatch — record real-world profits paired with falling stock prices — rattled semiconductor stocks across Asia and the US, including Micron and Applied Materials. Some of the anxiety was compounded by reports that **Nvidia is discussing a $250 billion financing guarantee** to help OpenAI build a giant new Ohio data center, and that Chinese rival chipmaker CXMT saw its own shares surge — both signs to some investors that AI capital spending is entering a riskier, more speculative phase.
key_points: SK Hynix's Q2 operating profit **jumped 557%** year-on-year to about **$41.6 billion** — yet its stock fell **9.6%** in a single day.
Samsung forecast a roughly **19-fold jump** in quarterly operating profit, driven by AI-driven memory chip demand.
SK Hynix's results still **missed analyst estimates** (₩60.54tn vs ₩64tn expected), with **no timeline** given for returning cash to shareholders.
The plunge came as **China's CXMT** chipmaker surged in its own listing and Nvidia explored a **$250 billion financing deal** for OpenAI, stoking fears the AI boom is overheating.
Samsung separately warned the global memory **chip shortage will last until 2028**, even as its own profits soar.

depth.background: For the past two years, memory-chip makers like Samsung and SK Hynix have ridden an unprecedented boom: every AI data center needs huge amounts of **high-bandwidth memory (HBM)** — specialized chips that feed data to AI processors like Nvidia's GPUs — and supply has struggled to keep up. That scarcity let chipmakers charge premium prices and post record profits quarter after quarter. But investors have grown increasingly nervous that Big Tech's enormous spending on AI data centers — hundreds of billions of dollars a year — is a bubble that can't keep growing at this pace forever.

stories.title: Zelenskyy and Trump meet at the White House on Patriot missiles and reviving Ukraine peace talks
stories.what_happened: On **July 28**, Zelenskyy met Trump at the White House for their second sit-down this month, this time centered on securing **licenses for Patriot missile interceptor production** and discussing how to revive stalled Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations. Zelenskyy described the meeting as 'good' afterward. The trip overlapped with his attendance at **Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral** in Washington — Graham's final legislative push had been the Russia/Iran sanctions bill the Senate voted 86-12 to advance. Zelenskyy told reporters he felt energized by a string of recent, successful Ukrainian deep-strike operations reaching into Russian territory, framing them as new leverage heading into any negotiations.
key_points: Zelenskyy and Trump held their **second White House sit-down this month**, focused on Patriot missiles and reviving peace talks.
Discussions centered on **licenses for Patriot air-defense interceptor production** for Ukraine.
The visit coincided with Zelenskyy attending **Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral** — Graham's last legislative act helped push the Russia/Iran sanctions bill.
Zelenskyy cited recent **successful Ukrainian deep-strike operations** on Russian territory as new leverage.

depth.background: Russia's war on Ukraine has ground on for years, with Ukraine's air defense increasingly stretched thin against Russian missile and drone barrages — **Patriot interceptors**, made by US defense contractor RTX, are considered among the best systems for shooting down Russia's more advanced missiles, but supply has been limited and expensive. Zelenskyy has repeatedly traveled to Washington to lobby for both weapons and renewed US-brokered peace efforts, with talks stalling and restarting multiple times. The late **Senator Lindsey Graham** was one of the most vocal supporters in Congress of both arming Ukraine and sanctioning Russia and Iran; his death and funeral brought Zelenskyy back to Washington at the same time as separate US diplomacy over the Middle East war.

stories.title: Saudi Arabia joins US airstrikes on Iran-backed militias in Iraq for the first time
stories.what_happened: On **July 28**, US Central Command said American and Saudi forces carried out joint precision airstrikes on Iran-aligned militia sites across eastern Iraq. The strikes came in response to more than **30 drone attacks** in the prior 72 hours that Washington and Riyadh blame on Iran's Revolutionary Guard, including one that struck the Abqaiq crude-processing complex. Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces, a state-linked militia umbrella that includes several Iran-backed factions, said **at least 20 of its members were killed and 32 wounded**. This is the **first time Saudi Arabia has publicly claimed strikes inside Iraq** since the US-Iran war began, marking a significant widening of the countries directly involved in the fighting. President Trump said afterward he was prepared to hit Iran 'hard' if the drone attacks continue, raising the stakes further.
key_points: Saudi Arabia struck targets inside Iraq for the **first time since the war began**, alongside US forces.
The strikes followed **more than 30 Iranian-directed drone attacks** in 72 hours, including one on Saudi Aramco's **Abqaiq** facility.
Abqaiq processes about **7 million barrels of crude a day** — the world's largest single oil-stabilization plant.
Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces say **at least 20 fighters were killed** and 32 wounded in the strikes.
Trump has since **threatened to hit Iran 'hard'** in response to the escalation.

depth.background: Since fighting broke out between the **US and Iran** earlier this year, Iran has relied heavily on allied militias scattered across Iraq, Syria and Yemen — grouped loosely under the banner of the 'Axis of Resistance' — to strike US and allied interests without exposing Iran's own territory to retaliation every time. Saudi Arabia, though a rival of Iran for decades and host to major US basing, had until now stayed out of direct strikes inside Iraq, worried about inflaming its own Shia population and Iranian-backed groups on its border. That changed after Iranian-directed drones hit **Saudi Aramco's Abqaiq plant** — the same facility a 2019 attack knocked offline for days, briefly wiping out roughly 5% of global oil supply. Abqaiq being targeted again turns a regional proxy fight into a direct threat to Saudi Arabia's own oil revenue and global energy security.

stories.title: Uganda launches emergency food relief after drought kills 19 in Karamoja
stories.what_happened: Uganda's government began distributing emergency food aid this week after local leaders reported that **19 people died of starvation-related causes** in the Karamoja sub-region over the past seven days. The Office of the Prime Minister says it will hand out **9,419,610 kilograms** of maize flour and dried beans to **313,987 households** across 480 parishes in Karamoja's nine districts, with the hardest-hit areas prioritized first before the operation extends through **July and August**. Uganda's Parliament has approved **UGX 45 billion** (roughly $12 million) specifically for the emergency response. Officials say **8 of Karamoja's 9 districts** are affected, with an estimated **1.5 million people** facing food shortages and malnutrition after this season's crops failed for lack of rain. The government also plans to distribute **drought-resistant, early-maturing seeds** ahead of the next planting season, and UNICEF and the World Food Programme are supporting the response.
key_points: **19 people have died** of hunger-related causes in Uganda's Karamoja sub-region over the past week.
The government will distribute **9.4 million kilograms** of maize flour and beans to over **313,000 households**.
Parliament approved **UGX 45 billion** (~$12 million) for the emergency response.
The drought has hit **8 of Karamoja's 9 districts**, leaving **1.5 million people** facing food shortages.
**UNICEF and the World Food Programme** are joining the government's relief effort.

depth.background: Karamoja, in Uganda's semi-arid northeast, is one of the country's poorest and most drought-prone regions, where pastoralist and farming communities depend on rains that have grown increasingly unreliable. A prolonged dry spell this year caused **widespread crop failure** just as the region's food reserves from the last harvest ran low. Uganda's Office of the Prime Minister has run emergency relief operations in Karamoja before, but local leaders say this year's death toll — **19 people in a single week** — is unusually severe. The response is being coordinated with **UN agencies** that track famine risk across East Africa's drought-prone Horn and Sahel belt.

stories.title: UN says nearly 500 Afghan civilians killed in Pakistan-Afghanistan border fighting since October
stories.what_happened: UNAMA's latest human-rights report tallies casualties from cross-border fighting between October 2025 and the end of June 2026: 499 civilians killed and over 1,000 wounded on the Afghan side alone. The single deadliest incident was a Pakistani airstrike on a drug-treatment center in Kabul in March, which killed hundreds of civilians. The report also documents a pattern where rescuers digging through rubble after one strike were hit by a follow-up strike. Pakistan has not published its own civilian casualty count for fighting inside its territory.
key_points: **499 civilians killed** and **1,216 wounded** in Afghanistan by cross-border fighting between **October and June**.
Pakistan blames Afghanistan for harboring the **Pakistani Taliban (TTP)**, a claim Kabul denies.
The deadliest single strike hit a **Kabul drug-treatment center** in March, killing hundreds.
Amnesty International says the Kabul strike should be investigated as a possible **war crime**.
The report documents cases of rescuers being hit by a **second strike** while pulling victims from rubble.

depth.background: Since the Afghan Taliban retook power in 2021, Pakistan has accused it of sheltering the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a separate militant group waging an insurgency inside Pakistan that is ideologically aligned with, but distinct from, the Afghan Taliban government. Kabul denies harboring the group. Tensions have hardened into open cross-border airstrikes and clashes over the past several months, tracked by the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), the UN's human-rights monitoring body in the country.

stories.title: Supreme Court pushes for a standalone 'digital arrest' law and RBI holds on mule accounts
stories.what_happened: Hearing a matter on cyber fraud, the Supreme Court urged the Union government to formally define 'digital arrest' as a distinct criminal offence carrying stricter penalties, rather than leaving it to be prosecuted under general fraud law. The Court also asked the RBI to formally implement a standard operating procedure letting banks place temporary debit holds on accounts suspected of being used as money mules, and suggested that once there is a prima facie case built on reasoned evidence, the assets of those involved should be frozen to prevent further misuse.
key_points: Supreme Court urged the Centre to make **'digital arrest' scams** a **standalone criminal offence** with tougher punishment.
Court wants the **RBI** to set a formal procedure for **freezing suspected 'mule' bank accounts** used to launder scam money.
Judges suggested freezing suspects' assets once there is a **prima facie case**, based on reasoned evidence, before a full trial.
The push targets the gap where stolen money vanishes through rented accounts faster than police can trace it.

depth.background: "Digital arrest" scams — where fraudsters pose as police, customs, or income-tax officials on video calls and frighten victims into transferring money to avoid a fake 'arrest' — have exploded across India, costing citizens hundreds of crores of rupees. Courts have repeatedly flagged a legal gap: the fraud is prosecuted under generic cheating and IT-Act provisions rather than as its own crime, and the stolen money typically moves within hours through 'mule accounts' — bank accounts opened or rented out specifically to receive and quickly forward laundered funds — before it can be frozen.

stories.title: Sri Lanka Women complete series comeback, beat Pakistan by 8 wickets in the decider
stories.what_happened: Chasing a target of 188, Sri Lanka lost early wickets but Chamari Athapaththu's quickfire 52 off 38 balls and Harshitha Samarawickrama's unbeaten 71 off 92 balls carried the hosts home with more than 12 overs to spare. Athapaththu also took 3 for 27 with the ball earlier in the match. The win sealed the series 2-1 for Sri Lanka after they trailed 0-1.
key_points: Sri Lanka chased down **188** in **37.2 overs** to win the decider by **8 wickets** in Hambantota.
**Harshitha Samarawickrama** anchored the chase with an unbeaten **71 off 92 balls**, hitting 11 fours.
**Chamari Athapaththu** starred with both bat and ball: **52 off 38 balls**, plus **3 for 27**.
The win completes a **comeback series victory** after Pakistan had gone 1-0 up in the opener.
The result carries points in the ICC **Women's Championship (2025-29)**, which feeds World Cup qualification.

depth.background: Pakistan's women won the first ODI to go 1-0 up in the three-match series, but Sri Lanka hit back to level it before Tuesday's decider in Hambantota. Both sides are building toward the next ODI World Cup cycle, and every match in the ICC Women's Championship carries direct qualification points, which raises the stakes of an ordinary bilateral series.

stories.title: Ralf Schumacher claims Wolff deliberately lowballed Verstappen — Jos Verstappen calls it false
stories.what_happened: Schumacher said Wolff approached Verstappen with a contract offer structured to be financially unacceptable, calling it a deliberate move given Verstappen's price tag next to a cheaper, faster-rising Antonelli. Jos Verstappen dismissed the report as inaccurate in a public response. Neither Mercedes nor Red Bull has confirmed the details of any formal offer.
key_points: Ralf Schumacher claims Mercedes boss **Toto Wolff** made Max Verstappen a **lowball contract offer** — one so poor it was never really on the table.
Verstappen reportedly earns **$65-70 million a year** in base salary alone at Red Bull.
Schumacher suggests Wolff didn't actually want an expensive Verstappen alongside rising star **Kimi Antonelli**, who now **leads the championship**.
Verstappen's father **Jos Verstappen** publicly rejected the claim, saying Schumacher has it wrong again.
Verstappen sits sixth in the standings, roughly **110 points behind leader Antonelli**, in a difficult season by his usual standard.

depth.background: Verstappen holds a Red Bull contract exit clause that became active this summer, and rumors have swirled for months about where he races in 2027 — Mercedes, Aston Martin, or staying put at Red Bull have all been floated. Toto Wolff and Verstappen are reported to have held informal talks earlier in the season. Ralf Schumacher, a former F1 driver turned TV pundit, is a frequent and sometimes contested source of paddock claims. Antonelli, in just his first full season, has surged into the championship lead for Mercedes.

stories.title: France orders 4,000 more evacuated as a fresh heatwave threatens to reignite the Bordeaux wildfire
stories.what_happened: Firefighters held the Gironde fire in check through a calm night, containing flare-ups near coastal dunes and keeping the burned area steady at **420 square kilometers (162 square miles)**. But French authorities still ordered nearly **4,000 more people** evacuated Tuesday from tourist sites on the Atlantic coast, as rising heat and falling humidity threatened to undo that fragile hold. Officials described the fire as **'stabilized, not fixed'** — meaning it could flare up again as temperatures climb. Total evacuations from the France-Spain wildfire wave now stand at roughly **330,000 people**.
key_points: French authorities evacuated **~4,000 more people** Tuesday from Atlantic coast tourist sites near Bordeaux.
The fire has burned **420 square kilometers** — an area **four times the size of Paris**.
Officials call the blaze **'stabilized, not fixed'**: unchanged overnight, but returning heat could restart its spread.
It has already forced roughly **330,000 people** to evacuate across France and Spain combined since last week.

depth.background: A wildfire west of Bordeaux, in France's Gironde region, has been burning since last week, at times turning into a self-feeding **firestorm** that outran containment efforts. It's part of a broader wave of wildfires across southwestern Europe, driven by a **heat dome** that has baked the region for days. Yesterday's coverage noted **over 360,000 people** had already fled homes and vacation lets across France and Spain, prompting French President Macron to call an emergency government meeting.

thread.previously: Wildfires had already forced over 360,000 people to flee homes and vacation accommodation across southwestern France and Spain, prompting President Macron to call an emergency government meeting.
thread.changed: A fresh heatwave now threatens the fragile overnight containment near Bordeaux, prompting ~4,000 more evacuations even as the burned area itself held steady — officials call the fire 'stabilized, not fixed.'

stories.title: Protest leaders say the Centre has agreed to withdraw all NEET-crackdown cases nationwide, not just state by state
stories.what_happened: CJP spokesperson Saurav Das said the government has now agreed, after a nearly three-hour late-night meeting, to **withdraw FIRs**, **release detained protesters**, and **guarantee no further police action** against those involved in the anti-NEET agitation — a commitment CJP says came from the **Centre itself**, not just individual state governments. Draft notifications from Bihar and Assam were shared as templates guaranteeing case withdrawal, detainee release, and no future action. Bihar had already released 339 minors among 694 people detained during a July 25 bandh, while booking the remaining 355; Assam's five registered cases and 13 arrests are also being dropped.
key_points: The **Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)**, the youth group leading the protests, says the **Centre** has agreed to withdraw FIRs nationwide.
The claimed deal followed a **nearly three-hour late-night meeting** between CJP leaders and government representatives.
It would add **detainee releases** and a **guarantee against future police action** on top of what Bihar and Assam already did.
**Bihar** withdrew cases for incidents before **6am on July 26**; **Assam** logged **5 cases and 13 arrests** now being dropped.

depth.background: Weeks of protests over **NEET-UG paper-leak allegations** and a heavy-handed police response — including the July 20 crackdown and **RAF pellet-gun use** on demonstrators — forced Union Education Minister **Dharmendra Pradhan** to resign on July 25, with President Murmu accepting his resignation and Pralhad Joshi taking over the ministry as an additional charge. States began withdrawing cases against protesters one by one: **Bihar** first, then **Assam** as the second state, in moves already covered as the standoff eased.

thread.previously: Following Bihar, Assam became the second state to announce it would withdraw all cases against NEET-UG protesters and release detainees, easing (but not ending) the standoff over the July 20 police crackdown.
thread.changed: Protest leaders now say the Centre itself, not just individual states, has agreed after an all-night meeting to withdraw FIRs, release detainees, and guarantee no further action nationwide — a potential government-wide resolution rather than a state-by-state one.

stories.title: Defence PSU Bharat Electronics posts 9% profit jump as its order book crosses ₹72,000 crore
stories.what_happened: BEL's board approved and released its first-quarter results for the financial year 2026-27 (April-June 2026) on July 28. Consolidated net profit came in at ₹1,054.34 crore, up 9% from ₹969.91 crore in the same quarter last year, while revenue climbed a sharper 25.27% to ₹5,533.06 crore, showing the company converting its large order pipeline into billed work faster. The company's order book — contracts already signed but not yet delivered or billed — stood at ₹72,258 crore as of July 1, 2026, effectively multiple years of future revenue already secured. The board also raised the company's authorised capital to ₹1,000 crore, giving it more room to raise funds if needed. Brokerages including Motilal Oswal reaffirmed bullish ratings after the results.
key_points: **Bharat Electronics Ltd (BEL)**, India's state-run defence electronics maker, reported Q1 FY27 results on **July 28**
Consolidated net profit rose **9%** year-on-year to **₹1,054.34 crore**, from ₹969.91 crore a year earlier
Revenue jumped **25.27%** year-on-year to **₹5,533.06 crore**
Order book stood at **₹72,258 crore** as of July 1, 2026 — work already lined up for years ahead
Brokerage Motilal Oswal kept a 'Buy' rating with an unchanged target price of **₹510**

depth.background: BEL is a **Navratna** (top-tier) defence public sector undertaking under the Ministry of Defence, headquartered in Bengaluru, that makes radars, sonars, electronic-warfare systems, and communication equipment for India's armed forces. It has become a bellwether stock for India's push toward defence self-reliance (**"Atmanirbhar Bharat"** in defence manufacturing), which aims to cut costly imports of military hardware and build a domestic arms industry. India's overall defence production touched a record **₹1.78 lakh crore** in FY26, with exports near ₹39,000 crore, and BEL is one of the biggest contributors to that number.

stories.title: India's foreign secretary meets China's vice foreign minister in Beijing, both sides pledge to keep the border calm
stories.what_happened: On Monday, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri traveled to Beijing and held talks with China's Vice Foreign Minister Hua Chunying — the latest round of a diplomatic dialogue track that has run alongside military-level border talks since 2020. The two sides said they "acknowledged the importance of maintaining peace and tranquillity" in border areas, standard diplomatic language signaling neither wants a fresh flare-up, without claiming any new breakthrough on the actual territorial dispute. They reviewed the entire bilateral relationship and discussed advancing the Modi-Xi vision of India and China as **"development partners,"** touching on trade, economic ties, and people-to-people exchanges. Misri also met Sun Haiyan of the Chinese Communist Party's International Department to discuss political and academic exchanges. No new agreements, dates, or concrete deliverables were announced.
key_points: Foreign Secretary **Vikram Misri** met China's Vice Foreign Minister **Hua Chunying** in Beijing on **July 27**
Both sides acknowledged the importance of keeping **peace and tranquillity** along the disputed border
They reviewed the full bilateral relationship, from trade to culture, under the Modi-Xi 'development partners' framing
Misri separately met a senior Chinese Communist Party official, Sun Haiyan, for party-to-party exchanges
Comes as India runs a record **$151 billion** trade relationship with China but exports back only **$16.6 billion**

depth.background: India and China share a roughly 3,488-km disputed border called the **Line of Actual Control (LAC)**, and a deadly clash in Ladakh's Galwan Valley in June 2020 froze high-level ties for over four years. Relations began thawing after Prime Minister **Modi** met President **Xi Jinping** at the October 2024 **Kazan summit** (on the sidelines of a BRICS meeting in Russia), where both agreed troops should disengage from remaining friction points. Since then, direct flights have restarted, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has resumed, and border trade has reopened — but the two countries remain economically lopsided, with India heavily dependent on China for rare-earth magnets used in electronics and EVs.

stories.title: NASA's Swift Observatory catches a 'wandering' black hole shredding a star far outside its galaxy's core
stories.what_happened: Astronomers using the **Zwicky Transient Facility** at Palomar Observatory in Southern California first spotted an unusual brightening in a distant galaxy in **November 2025**. Follow-up observations with NASA's **Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory** and a network of other telescopes confirmed it as a tidal disruption event — a black hole devouring a star. The black hole responsible is estimated at **about 1 million solar masses**, and it sits roughly **30,000 light-years from the center** of its host galaxy, **WISEA J014656.04-152214.7**, itself about 750 million light-years from Earth. Swift's ultraviolet instrument measured the flare at temperatures near **54,000°F**, and at its peak the event briefly outshone the entire galaxy it occurred in. Researchers describe it as an apparent 'wandering' or 'orphan' black hole — one that ended up far from where supermassive black holes are normally expected.
key_points: Astronomers found a **supermassive black hole roughly 1 million times the Sun's mass** tearing apart a star **30,000 light-years off-center** in its host galaxy.
Supermassive black holes almost always sit at a galaxy's core — this is the **furthest off-center such event ever confirmed**.
The flare briefly outshone its **entire host galaxy in ultraviolet light**, reaching temperatures around **54,000°F (30,000°C)**.
The event was first flagged in **November 2025** by the Zwicky Transient Facility survey, then confirmed with NASA's **Swift Observatory**.
The host galaxy, **WISEA J014656.04-152214.7**, sits about **750 million light-years** from Earth.

depth.background: A **supermassive black hole** is an object millions to billions of times heavier than the Sun, found at the center of nearly every large galaxy, including our own Milky Way. When a star strays too close to one, gravity rips it apart in what astronomers call a **tidal disruption event (TDE)** — the shredded star's material heats up and glows brightly enough to be seen across billions of light-years. Because black holes at a galaxy's core are expected, finding one this far from the center is a genuine surprise that hints at a violent past for its galaxy.

stories.title: Shan Masood's century in vain as West Indies bowl Pakistan out for 282, taking a 29-run lead in the Trinidad Test
stories.what_happened: Pakistan resumed Day 3 at 199 for 3, with overnight batters Shan Masood and Salman Ali Agha looking to build a lead over West Indies' first-innings total of 311. The pair added 47 runs for the fourth wicket before Masood brought up his seventh Test century — and the first century ever scored at the Brian Lara Cricket Academy — before eventually being dismissed for 109 off 184 balls with 12 fours. Once Masood departed, West Indies' Justin Greaves ran through the rest of the batting order, finishing with figures of 5 for 27 in 11 overs, with support from Kemar Roach and Shamar Joseph, who took two wickets each. Pakistan were bowled out for 282 in 80.1 overs, falling 29 runs short of West Indies' 311, handing West Indies a first-innings lead heading into Day 4.
key_points: **Shan Masood** scored his **seventh Test century** (109 off 184 balls), the first-ever Test hundred at the newly-built **Brian Lara Cricket Academy** venue.
Pakistan, resuming Day 3 at 199/3, were eventually **bowled out for 282**, falling short of West Indies' first-innings total of 311.
West Indies all-rounder **Justin Greaves** ran through the Pakistan tail with **5 wickets for 27 runs**, his best Test bowling figures.
West Indies now hold a **29-run first-innings lead** heading into Day 4 of the series-opening Test.
Masood, playing his first innings since being relieved of Pakistan's captaincy, anchored the innings with a **155-run partnership** with Imam-ul-Haq before the tail folded quickly.

depth.background: This is the first Test of a two-match series between Pakistan and hosts West Indies, being played at the Brian Lara Cricket Academy in Tarouba, Trinidad — the ground's first-ever international red-ball match. Shan Masood was recently removed as Pakistan's Test captain after a run of poor results, making this century, his first innings as a specialist batter rather than skipper, personally significant as he tries to justify his place in the side on batting alone. West Indies' Justin Greaves is a fast-bowling all-rounder who has been growing into a senior bowling role for the hosts.

thread.previously: West Indies were bowled out for 311 on Day 2 after reaching 303/7 at lunch, with Shai Hope's unbeaten 89 the key contribution; Pakistan closed Day 2 at 60/1 in reply, still 251 runs behind.
thread.changed: Pakistan built on that platform through Day 3 — Masood converted a fifty into a century — but were eventually bowled out for 282, handing West Indies a 29-run first-innings lead rather than the deficit narrowing further.

stories.title: MI London beat Southern Brave Men off the final ball in a Hundred thriller at Southampton
stories.what_happened: Southern Brave Men posted 129 for 9 in their 100 balls, with Jamie Smith top-scoring with 49 as Trent Boult (2/15) and other MI London bowlers kept the total in check. Chasing, MI London got home with three wickets and just one ball to spare, with Will Jacks making 54 to anchor the pursuit before Ollie Pope sliced the winning runs — a two through backward point off the final delivery — to seal a three-wicket win. Marcus Stoinis had earlier taken 3 for 17 in the Southern Brave innings. The result was Southern Brave's third defeat of the competition, while MI London's win lifted them to third place in the men's table. The match capped a thrilling day of Hundred cricket at Southampton, after the venue's women's fixture between the same two clubs also went to the final overs, with Southern Brave's women winning by just 1 run.
key_points: **MI London** chased down Southern Brave's total with a **three-wicket win off the final ball**, with Ollie Pope steering the winning runs through backward point.
**Will Jacks** top-scored for MI London with **54** to anchor the chase of Southern Brave's 129/9.
**Jamie Smith** top-scored for Southern Brave with **49**, but the innings stalled as MI London's bowlers, led by **Marcus Stoinis (3/17)**, kept the total below 130.
The result is Southern Brave Men's **third loss** of the competition, while MI London moves up to **third place** in the table.
It came on the same day the two clubs' women's teams also played a nail-biter at the same Southampton venue, with Southern Brave's women winning by just 1 run.

depth.background: The Hundred is a franchise cricket tournament in English cricket, with each innings limited to 100 balls instead of the usual 120 in T20 cricket, designed for a shorter TV window and to attract new fans. Eight city-based men's and women's teams compete in parallel each season; Southern Brave, based in Southampton, and MI London, a newer franchise backed by the Mumbai Indians ownership group, are two of the eight teams. Both clubs' men's and women's sides played at the same Southampton venue on the same day, giving the ground a rare doubleheader.

stories.title: US and Iran edge toward a formal ceasefire deal, with the Strait of Hormuz the last sticking point
stories.what_happened: Regional mediators say they've made genuine headway getting US and Iranian officials back to the table after the fighting paused. The emerging shape of a deal centers on the Strait of Hormuz: rather than Iran ceding full control, it would be allowed to **run vessel-transit management through the strait with fewer restrictions on ships** than the US originally wanted — a face-saving compromise for Tehran. President Trump said the US held off on resuming strikes **because Iran asked it to**, while making clear the US remains ready to hold Iran to account if talks collapse. Muddying the picture, Iran's Foreign Ministry told reporters there are **no current negotiations** taking place — a direct contradiction of the mediators' account. Meanwhile the ceasefire remains fragile in practice: Saudi Arabia intercepted and shot down drones this week fired by Iran-backed militia groups operating out of Iraq, a reminder that the wider network of Iran-aligned armed groups across the region hasn't stood down.
key_points: Mediators report **real progress** reviving talks after nearly two weeks of direct US-Iran fighting.
The sketched compromise would let Iran manage ship traffic through the **Strait of Hormuz** with **fewer restrictions**, instead of the US demanding open access outright.
President Trump says Washington paused renewed strikes **at Iran's request**, but warns they resume if no deal is reached.
Iran's Foreign Ministry publicly denies any active negotiations are underway — the two sides are not yet aligned on the basic facts.
Even with a pause, Iran-backed militia drones are still flying: **Saudi Arabia shot down drones** fired at it from Iraq this week.

depth.background: In early July 2026, a rapid escalation between the US and Iran turned into the most direct fighting between the two countries in decades, with US strikes on Iranian targets and Iranian retaliation that spilled into the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which **about a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments pass** every day. Iran responded to strikes by asserting more control over the strait and firing on vessels, which is what sent oil prices spiking and then, on hopes of a ceasefire, tumbling nearly 7% (as covered here yesterday). A truce has technically been holding for over a week, but the two sides have not yet signed anything formal.

thread.previously: Yesterday, oil prices sank nearly 7% as the ceasefire held and Tehran opened talks on the Strait of Hormuz, with early signs the two sides were moving toward de-escalation.
thread.changed: Today mediators say real progress is being made on a Hormuz vessel-transit compromise, but Iran's own Foreign Ministry is publicly denying any negotiations are happening — and Saudi Arabia just shot down Iran-backed militia drones, showing the ceasefire is still fragile on the ground.
